# Task Registry

Every task needed to implement [`SCALE-ARCHITECTURE-PLAN.md`](SCALE-ARCHITECTURE-PLAN.md),
[`MONGO-MODULE-PLAN.md`](MONGO-MODULE-PLAN.md) and [`RELATIONAL-MODEL-PLAN.md`](RELATIONAL-MODEL-PLAN.md).

**This registry is derived mechanically from those documents** — one task per collection, per array
that must be split, per endpoint that must change, per UI surface that must stop loading eagerly.
§9 is a completeness matrix mapping every plan section to the task IDs implementing it: a decision
with no task is visible there rather than lost.

## How to read a task

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| **ID** | stable, never reused. `DB-*` database, `ING-*` ingest, `MID-*` middle layer, `UI-*` front end, `ANA-*` analyser, `INF-*` infrastructure, `CALL-*` JAR-analyzer call-tree/collection-attribution tracing (§109) |
| **Blocked by** | task IDs that must be done first. Empty means startable now |
| **DoD** | a **command and an expected result**, not an opinion |
| **Tests** | ships in the *same* increment (see `TEST-STRATEGY.md` §1) |

## Rules

1. **A task is one sitting.** If it cannot be finished in a few hours, split it.
2. **No task is "done" without its tests.** There is no testing phase at the end.
3. **Every DoD is executable.** If it cannot be checked by running something, rewrite it.
4. **Order is by dependency, not by preference.** The `Blocked by` column is the schedule.
5. **Ordering rule from the user: DB first.** `DB-*` and `ANA-*` precede `MID-*`, which precedes
   `UI-*`. (`ANA-001` was the exception; it is withdrawn — the bug it addressed does not exist, and
   comes before most `DB-*` work.

## Status legend

`TODO` · `WIP` · `DONE` · `BLOCKED` — this document is the single source of truth for status.

```
INF-001 module skeleton┘                            └──► DB-1xx dedup ──┘
```

| **P0 Foundations** | `INF-001..004` | module builds in the reactor |

## 1. P0 — Foundations

| ID | Title | Files | Blocked by | DoD (command → expected) | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

> **ANA-001 / ANA-002 / ANA-003 — WITHDRAWN, the premise was false.**
>
> These were raised on the basis that PL/SQL analysis is non-deterministic: `51 / 11 / 51` joins
> measured for one node across three runs. Re-checked against all four ORACLE runs on disk, the
> real sequence is `[11, 51, 51, 51]` — and the `11` is the **oldest** run, produced by a
> **different build**, before the join-attribution and statement-capture fixes landed.
>
> Comparing only the three runs from the same build: **0 of 18 `ERP_PRODUCT` nodes differ**. The
> analyser is deterministic. The variation was a code change being read as randomness.
>
> This mattered: ANA-001 was P0 and blocked the dedup lever, so the whole registry was sequenced
> behind a bug that does not exist. `ANA-003` (canonical ordering of emitted arrays) is still
> *worth doing* on its own merits — deterministic output is what makes content-addressed dedup
> reliable — but it is a nice-to-have, not a P0 blocker, and is re-filed as `DB-901`.
>
> (The same error appears in `CODING-STANDARDS.md` §9.2–9.3, which cites this bug as motivation.
> The determinism *test* it proposes is still worth having; the bug it cites is not real.)

| ~~ANA-001 | Make PL/SQL analysis deterministic (`tables[].joins` varies run to run) | `plsql-parser/.../flow/ChunkedFlowWriter.java`, join-attribution code | — | Run the ORACLE analysis 3×; `diff -r` the three `api/` trees → identical. Today run0/run2 report 51 joins on `ERP_PRODUCT` and run1 reports 11 | `DeterminismTest`: analyse twice in-process, assert byte-equal artifacts. Must fail if a `HashMap` iteration is reintroduced~~ *(withdrawn — see note above)* |
| ~~ANA-002 | Find and document the non-determinism root cause | same | ANA-001 | A written finding naming the class and mechanism; linked from `SCALE-ARCHITECTURE-PLAN.md` §A.2 | —~~ *(withdrawn — see note above)* |
| ~~ANA-003 | Canonical ordering for all emitted arrays | `ChunkedFlowWriter.java` | ANA-001 | Arrays whose order is not semantic are sorted by a stable key; order-bearing arrays (§B.2) documented as such | `CanonicalOrderTest`~~ *(withdrawn — see note above)* |

The join-multiplication interaction that regressed `JoinLeftTableResolutionTest` on the first two attempts is understood and fixed: a multi-table statement produces one `TableOperationInfo` per table it touches, all sharing identical `sqlText` but *different* `line` numbers (measured with a debug dump before fixing, not assumed) — the visitor's own native population puts the statement's full join list on exactly one sibling, so join-carry now (a) is skipped entirely for any op whose statement (`sqlText` alone — `line` cannot be part of the key) already has native joins on a sibling, and (b) is scoped to the op's own table when it does run, the same criterion `ownedBy` already applies to columns | none | `enrich()`/`coverage()` produce identical column/predicate/join/DDL counts whether a procedure is standalone or package-body-contained; `JoinLeftTableResolutionTest` stays exactly 3, not 12 or 6 | `PackageBodyEnrichmentTest` (3), `JoinLeftTableResolutionTest` (1, unchanged), `DynamicDdlActionTest` (4, unchanged) |

## 13. Two P7 rows re-sized against reality

`UI-003` and `UI-004` were written against a payload that **no longer exists**, and doing them as
worded would now be work in the wrong place.

Both were sized when the class tree carried member arrays. MID-018 made `members=false` the default
on every fork, so the same 1,633 classes are:

| | with members | lean |
|---|---|---|
| measured JAR (1,633 classes) | **24.5 MB** | **0.9 MB** |
| per class | ~15 KB | **575 bytes** |
| at 10,000 classes | ~150 MB | 5.8 MB |
| at 100,000 classes | ~1.5 GB | 57.5 MB |

**`UI-004` — "remove the 11.8 MB unpaged fallback".** That fallback now fetches ~0.9 MB, and it only
runs when the paged source is unavailable (a stale `page-envelope.js`). Deleting it removes a working
safety net to save a payload 13× smaller than the one that justified the task.

**`UI-003` — "no 100,000-class array".** The drain loop still builds one array of every class, but at
575 bytes each that is 57.5 MB at 100,000 classes rather than the ~1.5 GB the row was written
against. And the drain is **load-bearing**: three view modes (`renderProjectView`,
`renderVisualView`, the package view's `_groupBySourceJar`) and the JAR-source filter each read every
class. A project view that renders a subset is a wrong answer, not a faster one.

Removing it is therefore the same shape as MID-003 — a vertical slice per view mode, converting each
to a server-side aggregate — for a 57.5 MB worst case at a class count nobody has validated. That is
a poor trade against the P6 work still outstanding.

**Recommendation:** leave both at ◐ with these numbers recorded, and revisit if a JAR with >10,000
classes appears. The 27× that mattered has already been taken.

*The general point:* a task list written against measurements ages as the measurements change. Two
rows here were still describing a 24.5 MB payload that a task three sections earlier had reduced to
0.9 MB. Re-measuring before implementing is cheaper than implementing and then discovering the
justification moved.

## 14. The four remaining P6 endpoint slices, measured before starting

Following §13's lesson, all four were measured first. **Three should not be done as worded; one
should.**

| task | measured today | growth path | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MID-004` `/call-graph` → paged edges | 0.26 MB, **847 edges** | edges grow with call density: **35,776 at 832 procedures** in the load proof, so ~344,000 and ~100 MB at 8,000 | **do it** — the only one with a measured growth path |
| `MID-005` `/resolver/{type}` → paged | 0.22 MB across 80 files, **largest 30 KB** | scales with distinct objects; ~4.6 MB total at 154× | not worth paging a 30 KB response |
| `MID-009` `/source/{file}` → range-read | reads **one** file, largest **94.3 KB** | a procedure's source does not grow with the corpus — the *count* does, and each request fetches one | not worth it; "no `readAllBytes`" is guarding a 94 KB read |
| `MID-017` `/correction-logs`, `/run-logs`, `/catalog` → paged | **no data exists** — 0 corrections directories, 0 catalog collections | unknown | unmeasurable here; these list files that have never been produced in this dataset |

**`MID-009` is worth a note.** Its DoD is "No `readAllBytes`", which reads like a memory rule but is
guarding a single 94 KB file. The concern it *should* address is different: the source viewer needs
line ranges to jump to a line without transferring the whole file — a feature requirement, not a
size one. Re-word it that way or close it.

**`MID-017` cannot be assessed from this repository.** The endpoints enumerate correction and run
logs, and no analysis on disk has ever produced any. Paging an empty list is pointless, and there is
no evidence of the size it reaches in use. It needs either production data or a decision that the
feature is dormant.

## 15. MID-004 — the render was capped, the transfer was not

FE-018 capped the graph **renderer** at 300 nodes, because the all-pairs repulsion step over 200
frames is ~6.4 billion operations at 8,000. The **transfer** was never capped: the client fetched
every edge and discarded almost all of them.

| | edges |
|---|---|
| measured today | 847 |
| load proof, 832 procedures | **35,776** |
| extrapolated, 8,000 procedures | ~344,000 (~100 MB) |

All of it fetched to draw 300 nodes.

`/call-graph/top?limit=300` returns the highest-degree subgraph. **Selection has to be server-side**:
the criterion is degree, degree is a property of the whole graph, and a client cannot pick the top
300 without first holding all of it — which is the transfer being avoided.

Four decisions in it worth keeping:

- **Degree counts both directions.** A procedure called by many and one that calls many are both
  hubs, and a reader opening a call graph is looking for hubs.
- **Both endpoints must survive.** An edge to a dropped node draws a line to nothing.
- **`truncated`, `totalNodes` and `totalEdges` travel with the response.** A subgraph presented as a
  graph is precisely the failure FE-018's notice exists to prevent, and dropping these counts would
  reintroduce it one layer down.
- **The old route is kept, not 410'd** as MID-004 asks. It has two live consumers: this visualisation
  and `export.js`, which needs every edge because an export of part of a graph is wrong. Bounding the
  export is FE-019's problem.

`CallGraphTopNTest`, 8 assertions. Calibrated: degree counting one direction (4 fail), edges kept
with one endpoint (2), truncation not reported (1), one field spelling understood (1).

**A calibration that could not fire, and what replaced it.** Dropping the explicit name tiebreaker
left the determinism test passing, because `HashMap` iteration order is stable for a given key set
within a JVM. The test now asserts the property it *can* prove — the slice does not depend on the
order edges arrived in — and states in a comment that the tiebreaker's own effect is not
demonstrable in-process. The tiebreaker stays: `HashMap` ordering is not contractual, so without it
the slice is only incidentally stable. Saying that plainly is better than an assertion that implies
more than it checks.

**Client half done.** `callGraphViz` fetches `/call-graph/top?limit=MAX_SIMULATED_NODES` and takes
the total from the server's own `truncated`/`totalNodes`, because when the server slices before
sending, the client never sees the real count — reporting what *arrived* would say "showing 300 of
300" on a graph of 8,000. A notice that is technically present and tells the reader nothing is worse
than none, because it looks like the feature works.

The **client-side cap is kept** as a second line of defence. The server bounds the response now, but
a stale deploy or a direct call to the old route can still deliver an unbounded one, and a renderer
that depends on someone else having been careful is one deploy away from a hung tab.

`getCallGraph()` stays for `export.js`. Three client assertions added to `graph-ceiling.test.mjs`,
calibrated: viz reverting to the whole fetch (1 fail), the server total ignored (1), the local cap
removed (2 fail).

*A test bug worth noting:* the new assertions used `excludes`, which that file had never imported —
so the first run failed with a `ReferenceError` rather than an assertion. A test that throws is not
a test that fails, and the two read very differently in the output.

## 16. MID-101 / MID-102 — re-scoped; the remaining callers are legitimate

MID-101 says "migrate the 8 `PersistenceService.load()` callers". After MID-013 and MID-014 the
**request-path** callers are gone. What remains is not the same defect:

| remaining | count | why it needs the whole analysis |
|---|---|---|
| `ClaudeJobExecutor` | 6 | a background job that enriches and re-saves the analysis; nothing is waiting on a response |
| `ClaudeController./versions/load-static` | 1 | switches the **active** analysis; the whole result is what `setLatestResult` holds |
| `ClaudeController.mergeNewFindings` | 1 | merges findings into the static analysis to produce a new one; needs every table operation to deep-copy |

The defect MID-013 fixed was **49.4 MB read per request to return 3.8 KB**. None of these is that: six
are background work with no request attached, and two are whole-analysis operations by nature — a
mode switch and a merge. Migrating them would mean restructuring the version-switch and the Claude
merge into streaming forms, which is a different and much larger task than "migrate the callers".

**MID-102 ("delete `load()` / `loadStatic()` / `rehydrate()`") is therefore not achievable as
worded** while those eight exist.

*A correction to my own working, recorded because the method was the point:* I first reported
`rehydrate()` as having **zero references** and therefore deletable. It has two — it is a private
helper inside `jar-analyzer-core`'s `PersistenceService`, and my grep covered only `unified-web`. I
measured one module and generalised to the repository, which is the identical mistake as the
`sourceMap` projection in §13 (one screen's fields generalised to all consumers). Both times the
error was optimistic, and both times a wider grep was the whole fix.

**Recommendation:** re-word MID-101 as "no `load()` on a request path" — which is **already true** —
and split the streaming redesign of the version-switch and Claude merge into its own row, sized
separately. MID-102 stays blocked behind that.


---

## 17. A systematic error in my own audit — planned collection names

The §11 audit marked ING rows done on the evidence of **populated collections**. That was the right
kind of evidence and the wrong reading of it: `Splitter` names a child collection after its parent
and field (`am_parent__field`), so the data was there under a name the plan never specified. I checked
that rows existed and not that the *planned* rows existed.

Found by a different route — `IdCodec.dbColumn()` is declared and never called, which is the same
"declared but never wired" shape as the `am_txn_statement` defect. Pulling that thread: of 58
collection names the plan uses, **26 do not appear anywhere in the ingest module**.

*(Corrected: those names live in `SCALE-ARCHITECTURE-PLAN.md`, not `PLAN-04`. I wrote
PLAN-04 from memory when first recording this and did not check — the same shortcut as
the `rehydrate()` and `IdCodec.of()` errors, and caught the same way, by grepping.)*

### Stored, under a different name (13)

The data is present and reachable via `parentRef`; only the name differs.

| plan | actual |
|---|---|
| `am_column_usage` | `am_statement__columns` |
| `am_predicate` | `am_statement__predicates` |
| `am_stmt_join` | `am_statement__joins` |
| `am_method_parameter` | `am_java_method__parameters` |
| `am_method_field_access` | `am_java_method__field_accesses` |
| `am_method_string_literal` | `am_java_method__string_literals` |
| `am_annotation` | `am_java_class__annotations`, `am_java_method__annotations` |
| `am_class_interface` | `am_java_class__interfaces` |
| `am_db_column` | `am_db_object__db_columns` |
| `am_db_constraint` | `am_db_object__db_constraints` |
| `am_db_index` | `am_db_object__db_indexes` |
| `am_db_trigger` | `am_db_object__db_triggers` |
| `am_subtree_used_by` | `am_subtree_table__used_by_nodes` |

### Genuinely absent, on rows marked done (5 rows)

Re-marked **◐**: `ING-014` (`am_cursor_object`, `am_cursor_unresolved`), `ING-017`
(`am_sequence_obj`), `ING-019` (`am_ddl_action`), `ING-106` (`am_java_field_constant`), `ING-112`
(`am_endpoint_pool_link`). Each row delivered part of what it names.

### Why it matters, and why it is not data loss

Nothing is lost — every row is stored and reachable. But **P6 is specified against the plan's
names**, so a middle-layer query written to `am_db_column` returns zero rows against a fully
populated database. That is the `am_txn_statement` failure mode exactly: every integrity check
passes, the round trip passes, and the answer is empty.

**Decided 2026-09-07 — the plan changed, not the code.** `SCALE-ARCHITECTURE-PLAN.md` now uses the
`am_parent__field` names `Splitter` actually produces (8 references), and carries a note explaining
why. The reason for choosing this direction: a derived name cannot drift from the data, whereas a
hand-written name per collection needs an override map in `Splitter` maintained for every new split
field forever — which is the class of gap that produced this discrepancy.

Two consequences, both applied:

- `IdCodec.dbColumn()` was kept undeleted only to avoid pre-empting this decision. With the
  decision made it is genuinely dead and **deleted**.
- The plan's index spec for the statement children read `{stmtRef: hashed}`. `stmtRef` exists
  nowhere in the codebase — `Splitter` writes `parentRef` — so that index would have been built on
  an absent field. Corrected to `{parentRef: hashed}`. Found only because renaming the collections
  made me read the row it sits on, which is an argument for doing renames by hand.

The 5 rows re-marked ◐ above are **unaffected**: those collections are genuinely absent, not
renamed, and remain open work.

*One contradiction spotted alongside:* `TablesIndexMapper` documents `dbColumns`, `dbConstraints`
and `dbIndexes` as deliberately **embedded** — measured at 1.2 columns per object, worst case ~40,
bounded and always read with the parent. The no-arrays rule split them out anyway. The measured
rationale is sound and the comment is now describing something that does not happen; Resolved: the
comment now carries a `<b>Correction.</b>` block stating that the measured rationale holds and is
not what happens, and why the invariant wins — "bounded today" is a property of the data, and an
embedded array is one schema change from being unbounded.


## 18. The MongoDB driver upgrade — 4.11.2 to 5.2.1

Decided and done 2026-09-07. The row asked for it so "the 50 remaining `maxTimeMS` call sites
collapse to one setting". That is not what happened, and the difference matters more than the
upgrade.

### What the upgrade actually gives

One client-wide operation timeout, set once in `MongoConnection` at `QueryBudget.BATCH_MS`. Every
operation this application issues is now bounded — **including the ones nobody budgeted**. That is
the chokepoint `QueryTimeoutGateTest` said did not exist, and it also covers server selection, so
`MongoConnection.open` can no longer stall on a dead server.

### The trap it opened, which nearly shipped

Under CSOT the server **ignores** `maxTimeMS`. Measured on 5.2.1 against a 200,000-document
unindexed scan:

| configuration | outcome |
|---|---|
| `maxTime=1ms`, no client timeout | REJECTED `MongoExecutionTimeoutException` |
| `maxTime=1ms`, client timeout 300 s | **COMPLETED in 59 ms** — budget discarded |
| `withTimeout=1ms`, client timeout 300 s | REJECTED `MongoOperationTimeoutException` |
| no budget, client timeout 1 ms | REJECTED `MongoOperationTimeoutException` |

Row 2 is the finding. Setting the client timeout and leaving the existing
`.maxTime(QueryBudget.REQUEST_MS, …)` calls in place would have widened **every 15-second request
budget to 300 seconds**, with nothing failing, nothing logged, and 18 call sites still reading as
budgeted. A guard that is present and enforces nothing — the exact failure this registry has now
recorded ten times.

So `QueryBudget` moved from wrapping iterables to wrapping collections (`withTimeout`, which CSOT
honours), all 18 sites were converted, and `.maxTime(` is now **banned outright** in main code
rather than ratcheted — a call that looks like a budget and is ignored is worse than no call.

### Three things found on the way, none of them the task

1. **The bump silently didn't take.** Only `mongodb-driver-sync` is declared anywhere, so pinning
   it resolved sync 5.2.1 against `driver-core` 4.11.2 and `bson` 4.11.2 — two driver versions on
   one classpath, which `analyzer-storage/pom.xml` already records as a *runtime* failure. It
   compiled cleanly; `MongoClientSettings` simply had no `timeout()` method, because that class
   lives in core. The fix is overriding Spring Boot's managed `mongodb.version`, which the BOM
   applies to all four artifacts together. Three modules had each declared the literal `4.11.2`
   independently, and the comment claiming they were "pinned to each other" prevented nothing.
2. **`QueryBudget`'s entire helper API was dead.** All six iterable-wrapping methods had zero
   callers, and `BATCH_MS` had none either — every site inlined `.maxTime(...)` instead. Its
   carefully argued "two budgets" design had never been built. Fourth instance of "declared but
   never wired", and the reason the class is now one method.
3. **`{stmtRef: hashed}`** in `SCALE-ARCHITECTURE-PLAN.md` — an index on a field that exists
   nowhere in the codebase (`Splitter` writes `parentRef`). Found only because the §17 rename made
   me read the row it sits on.

### The gate's justification expired, and it is still there

`QueryTimeoutGateTest`'s original reason — an unbudgeted query can hang forever — is **gone**. The
50 sites are still wrong for a smaller reason: they run on the 300-second batch floor, which is
right for ingest and far too long for a request. The count is unchanged at 50 across 17 files
(counting `QueryBudget.request(` instead of `maxTime(` changed no number), and the two
request-path files remain at zero. Recorded rather than quietly kept, because a gate whose stated
reason has expired is how a list outlives its problem — the same lesson as §13, §14 and §17.


## 19. Closing the five rows §17 re-marked — four fixed, one blocked upstream

§17 found five rows marked done whose collections did not exist. Each was checked against the
source artifacts before anything was written, because the §17 lesson was precisely that a plan name
is not evidence.

| row | collection | what was actually there | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| ING-112 | `am_endpoint_pool_link` | positional integers, no reference | **fixed** — 60,483 resolved links |
| ING-014 | `am_cursor_object` | table names as bare strings | **fixed** — 1,103 rows with `objectRef` |
| ING-017 | `am_sequence_obj` | sequences existed only as two string columns | **fixed** — 14 entities |
| ING-106 | `am_java_field_constant` | constant already stored whole on the field | **not created** — see below |
| ING-019 | `am_ddl_action` | nothing: the parser emits no DDL | **blocked upstream** |

### The same defect, three times

All three fixes are one defect wearing different clothes: **a reference stored as a value**.

- An endpoint's pool references were `{value: 7}` — a position with nothing tying it to a pool, a
  run, or anything else. Rebuilding `am_endpoint_pool~<jar>~beans~7` was every caller's problem.
- A cursor's tables were `{value: "ERP_CUSTOMER"}`.
- A sequence use carried `schemaName` and `sequenceName` and nothing to resolve them.

In each case the data was complete, every integrity check passed, and the reverse question — *which
endpoints use this bean, which cursors read this table, which sequences does this system have* — had
no reference to match and no index to use. `OrphanRefChecker` discovers fields ending in `Ref`, so
across all three there were **~61,600 references it could not see**. That is the `am_txn_statement`
shape: present, consistent, and unqueryable.

All three now emit a resolved key, and all three are checked automatically because of how discovery
works — no new checker code.

**Rows moved rather than multiplied.** The positional and string-valued rows are removed from the
parent *before* `Splitter` sees it, so the counts are unchanged: 47,461 + 9,264 + 3,758 = 60,483
links, and 1,103 cursor tables. Storing both shapes would put the same fact in two places, which is
how a query gets written against the wrong one.

### Two rows that should not be built, and why that is not the same as skipping them

**`am_java_field_constant`** — the constant belongs to the field, is read with it, and has no
identity of its own. A collection holding a projection of one field would be the same fact twice.
But the row's *verification* was missing: it cited `ConstantNotTruncatedTest`, and **that class did
not exist**. Written now: the largest constant is compared byte for byte against the source (21,845
bytes, an ANTLR serialised ATN), all 52 are counted, and nothing is allowed to sit at a power-of-two
length where a truncation would land. Calibration: truncating at 1,024 bytes fails two of the three.

**`am_ddl_action`** — no DDL data exists anywhere in the artifacts. Not thin, not renamed: absent.
The row is left ◐ and attributed upstream, because building an empty collection would make the
registry read complete while answering nothing. Same reasoning as `am_cursor_unresolved`, which
would have zero rows on any corpus where every cursor table resolves — and all 1,103 do.

### The tenth guard that guarded nothing

`CursorResolutionTest` asserts that an unresolvable cursor table keeps its name and gets no
reference. It **cannot fail**. Calibration proved it: changing the writer to guess a schema —
`schemas.getOrDefault(name, "ANALYZER")`, the exact mis-attribution ING-014 forbids — left all six
tests green. Every cursor table in the corpus resolves, so the guessing branch is never taken, and
a test that iterates stored rows cannot observe a path the data never enters.

`CursorSchemaAttributionTest` supplies the input instead: a synthetic node with one resolvable table
and one that is not, mapped through a `DocSink` lambda with no database. Both mis-attribution
mutations now fail, and so does dropping the unresolvable row. The lesson is the same one recorded
nine times before, with a new edge on it: *a guard is only as good as the inputs the test can
produce*, and a corpus is not a test-input generator.

### One mistake worth keeping

I first wrote `objectRef` as `IdCodec.dbObject(ctx.runId(), schema, name)` — run-scoped. It looks
right: same recipe, same components. `am_db_object` is keyed by the **entity** key so that a table
dedups across runs, and `TablesIndexMapper` states the rule for children in a comment two lines
from the code I copied. All 26 distinct tables dangled, and nothing but `OrphanRefChecker`
distinguished the two forms — the run-scoped key is a perfectly well-formed string that addresses
nothing.


## 20. UI-016, and what re-anchoring §8 to the code turned up

`ys` after §19 meant "keep going", and P7 was legitimately next since the backend rows were closed.
The first thing that needed doing was not a fix.

### Most of §8.2 pointed at nothing

Every `file:line` in §8.2 was stale. The rows enumerate `PA.tf` call sites across per-module copies
of a table framework that now lives in one place — `shared/tableFramework.js`, `PA.tf` defined at
line 44 — and `tableFramework.js:229-279`, the path `UI-013` cites for the client filter/sort chain,
does not exist. Converting "the site at `joins.js:77`" when nothing is at that line means reading
the file and guessing what was meant.

Re-measured instead: **103 client filter/sort references across 26 files**, with 10 files already
reading from a page source — including two that appear in both lists, because they were converted
while keeping a client path for callers that had not been. §8.2 now carries that table rather than
the old site lists, and `UI-008`'s "verify `cursors.js` already paged" is confirmed: it is.

§8.3 held up by contrast: `callGraph.js:207` is exactly `_indexNodes`, and `expandAll` had drifted
only from 399 to 392. Worth saying, because "the list is stale" is a claim that has to be checked
per row rather than assumed once.

### UI-016 was not blocked

The row was blocked by `MID-006` — a capped server endpoint. It did not need one: the pre-walk was
a client-side traversal of a tree the client already had. It assigned every node a step number and
put it in `_nodeMap` before a single row was drawn, and the only readers of that map are a click
handler and the lazy branch builder, both reachable only from a row that was rendered. The parser
copy also set `_parentSourceFile` on every node, which nothing in that file reads — the `@line` link
is rendered from a separate structure built in `parser/js/app.js`. One field for a handler that
needed it lazily, one field for nobody.

Both copies now assign a step on first render, once, so a re-rendered node keeps the id its DOM was
built with. The `plsql` copy's doc comment had stated the objection to this — *"Numbering during
render would renumber every time something expanded"* — which is true of unconditional numbering and
answered by the idempotence guard. That copy also reset `stepCounter` to 0 immediately after its
walk while `renderNode` had a fallback that numbered from the counter, so any node reaching the
fallback would have been handed a step already in use. It was unreachable, because the walk and the
renderer both skip a `circular` node's children — but it was one disagreement away from opening the
wrong subtree, and lazy numbering removes the fallback and the reset together.

The whole-tree walk still exists, as `_countNodes`, called when the user clicks Expand All. The
expand-all prompt is a safety warning, and one that understates is worse than none: reading
`_nodeMap` after this change would have told a user that a 1,250-node trace has three.

### The eleventh guard that guarded nothing

The tests called `renderNode` directly. Calibration: I reinstated the eager walk in `render()` and
**all nine tests stayed green**, because none of them called `render()` — the function the walk
lives in. Identical to asserting a truncation notice by calling the notice function instead of the
layout that emits it. Driving `render()` instead required four DOM fixture elements the entry path
touches; with that, reinstating the walk fails four tests across the two files.

Two smaller versions of the same error on the way: the fixture first counted reads of the rendered
level rather than descents into the level below, and reported "800 of 400 leaves" against a renderer
that was walking nothing — `hasChildren` reads `node.children` twice per drawn row. And a missing
`PA.nodeIndex` stub failed with "Cannot read properties of undefined", which is a test that throws
rather than a test that fails.


## 21. UI-021 done, UI-020 withdrawn — both on the same measurement

### UI-021 was real, and not blocked

Marked blocked by `MID-016`, a server task. It needed nothing from the server: both offending walks
are client-side, over a tree the client already holds.

- `_renderTraceNode` recursed the whole tree into one HTML string. `showTrace`'s own comment
  measures that render at **120 MB** — and the fix applied at the time was to make repeat clicks a
  no-op. That addressed the queue of renders and left the first one unbounded, which is treating the
  symptom with the diagnosis already written down.
- `_flattenTree` guarded `depth > 50` and left breadth alone. A tree 50 deep is small; a tree three
  deep with a hundred thousand children per level is not. Identical to the defect FE-018 fixed in
  `_flattenOps`: **capping the dimension that was not the problem**, which reads as a bound and is
  not one.

Both now stop at `MAX_TRACE_NODES: 2000`, set equal to `JA.callGraph.MAX_FLATTENED_OPS` because the
two views sit beside each other and a reader should not have to discover that they stop at different
sizes. The notice reports the tree's real total via `_countTreeNodes`, and the node-nav fallback's
`totalNodes` does too — it would otherwise have reported the size of the slice, so a 300,000-node
endpoint would have claimed to have 2,000.

One ordering bug of my own, found before it shipped: I decremented the budget *above* the
pre-existing `depth > 25` check, so nodes skipped for being too deep still spent a row of the
budget, and the ceiling would arrive early on deep trees by exactly the number never drawn.

### UI-020 is withdrawn, and the reason is the same measurement

The row asks for windowed row rendering so the DOM stays bounded regardless of tree size. Measured
from `call_graph.json`: **max fan-out is 19** (`ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE`, 218 edges). With
`_initialDepth: 1`, one rendered level is at most 19 rows. Windowing that bounds nothing.

The real unbounded case was never a single level — it was the total rendered after Expand All, and
that is now gated by a confirm prompt whose count is accurate (§20). So the row's DoD is satisfied
by a different mechanism than the one it names, and building a window as well would add machinery
to bound 19 rows.

`UI-019` ("per-level lazy children from a paged endpoint") stays open: the client is already lazy
per level, but from the in-memory tree, so its DoD — *one level = one request* — genuinely needs the
server work.

**Fifth row in this registry withdrawn or re-scoped on re-measurement** (§13 twice, §14, §20's
`UI-005..012`, now `UI-020`). The pattern is consistent enough to state plainly: the task list was
written from a scale extrapolation, the code has since moved, and the extrapolated number is not
evidence about today. Re-measuring first has now changed the answer more often than not.


## 22. MID-007 — half delivered, half needs a decision that is not mine

### The half with no trade-off

`/search` called `readTree` on `api/statements/index.json` and cached the result. Measured on the
largest analysis (MYSQL, **7.0 MB**, 5,015 statements):

| | retained |
|---|---|
| `readTree` | **24.3 MB** |
| streaming | **~0 MB** |

24 MB for a 7 MB file is the ordinary cost of a `JsonNode` tree, not a Jackson defect. The defect is
holding it: statements scale with the analysed code, so at the stated 8,000 procedures this file is
roughly **1.1 GB**, about 3.7 GB parsed. No cache size fixes that, because the problem is one
document.

`StatementIndexStream` now walks the file once, yielding one statement at a time and picking up the
header scalars as it passes them. `StatementSearcher` takes an `Iterable<JsonNode>` — the *same
loop*, given its rows from somewhere else — so the streaming and array paths cannot drift. Two
search implementations that disagreed would show up as users finding different results for the same
query depending on how the page was served, which is worse than a slow search.

**The 24 MB memo is deleted, not resized.** Its reasoning was sound: "almost all" of a 13 ms search
was re-reading and re-parsing, so it cached one entry with a TTL. Streaming removes the thing being
cached, and with it the staleness the TTL guarded against — every request now reads the current
file, so an analysis re-run cannot be answered from the previous one.

### The half that changes what users find

The rest of the DoD is "`explain` shows `IXSCAN`", and that **cannot be delivered without changing
the search's answers**. `SearchQuery`'s default is a *substring* match, and no B-tree index can serve
`contains`. Making the query indexable means making it word- or prefix-based:

| today | indexable |
|---|---|
| `QTY` finds `TOTAL_QTY_ALLOCATED` | it would not |
| substring anywhere in the value | word or prefix only |

A user who types `QTY` and gets fewer rows than last week has had a feature removed, and no test in
this repository would fail. There is a second cost: `MongoPlsqlEntityIndex` stores statement
*counts* per node, not statements, so this is a new indexer rather than a new query — and the parser
search path reads artifacts, so the file path has to keep working regardless.

**Left open deliberately**, with the row re-marked ◐ and split into its two halves, because
"`IXSCAN`" is a performance target and "substring" is a product behaviour, and trading the second
for the first is a decision about the product.

### What it cost me to get the measurement right

My first heap assertion reported 12 MB and failed — measuring used heap before and after with no
collection in between, which counts the *churn* of 5,015 rows being created and dropped. That is
precisely what streaming is supposed to do. The code was correct and the test was wrong, and had I
trusted it I would have concluded the streaming did not work. It now collects on both sides, and
materialises the document in the same run for comparison, so the number has a scale rather than a
threshold.


## 23. The duplication rows were wrong in both directions

`UI-011` treats all of `plsql/js` as a duplicate framework; `UI-015` asks to consolidate "the three
duplicate pagers". Measured, neither holds.

### There is one pager, not three

`shared/page-envelope.js` defines the only `pageSource`, and `parser`, `plsql` and `jar` all load
it. The one module-specific pager left is `parser/js/pagination.js` (`PA.pager`). The consolidation
`UI-015` asks for has already happened — so the row is marked ☑ **and asserted**, because the
failure mode of a stale row like this is someone building a second shared pager to satisfy it.

### `plsql/js` is not a copy of `jar/js`

18 basenames are shared between the two trees. **None is byte-identical**, and most are not copies
in any useful sense:

| file | similarity |
|---|---|
| `app.js` | 0.7% |
| `summary-tables.js` | 2.9% |
| `callGraph.js` | 3.1% |
| `summary-helpers.js` | 34.0% |
| `summary-col-filter.js` | 90.5% |
| `summary-export-style.js` | 85.9% |

They are different implementations that happen to share a filename, which is a legibility problem —
a reader seeing one name twice will assume one thing — but not the deduplication task the row
describes. `UI-011` stays open with that correction recorded: its real content is the 26-file client
filter/sort chain in §8.2, not a merge.

### Two files that are genuinely the same code twice

`summary-col-filter.js` and `summary-export-style.js`. The plsql copies say so in their own header:
*"Domain-agnostic — identical to JAR version but uses PA namespace."* Normalising away the namespace
object and the escaper name (`JA.utils.escapeHtml` against `PA.esc`), the first pair is **exactly
identical** and the second differs only in four trailing comments the plsql side dropped.

**Not merged.** Sharing them needs an escaper indirection, and they drive column filtering and Excel
export on two pages with no behavioural tests over them — real risk for a cosmetic gain. What is
dangerous about a duplicate is not that it exists but that it **drifts**, leaving a fix in one copy
and the bug in the other. So the drift is now a failing test instead: the pair must stay
code-identical modulo namespace, and a new shared basename has to be declared deliberately.
Managed duplication rather than unmanaged.

### A hazard I checked and did not find

`jar/js/logviewer.js` against `parser`/`plsql`'s `logViewer.js` — different capitalisation of the
same name, which on a case-sensitive filesystem is a 404 waiting for a Linux deploy. Checked every
`<script src>`: each reference matches the case of its own file. Not a bug.

### The normaliser's own two mistakes

Stripping only lines that *begin* with `//` left trailing comments in place, so the two copies
differed by four `// strong blue` annotations — a diff that reads as drift and is nothing. Stripping
`//.*$` unconditionally would have eaten the `//` in a `'http://…'` literal and could make two
genuinely different files compare equal. It is a quote-aware scan, calibrated in both directions:
planting a real one-sided code change fails, planting a comment-only change does not, and a URL
inside a string survives.


## 24. UI-017 kept, UI-018 fixed — and a defect my own fix created

Both decided 2026-09-07.

### UI-017: `expandAll` stays

The row says "function gone, not warned about". Its concern was that the tree could be materialised
without the user asking. UI-016 addressed that differently: rendering is lazy, and the prompt now
reports an accurate whole-tree count, so the user opts in knowingly. Deleting a working feature to
satisfy the row's literal wording would remove the only way to see a whole trace. Closed as
satisfied by a different mechanism, with the mechanism named.

### UI-018: the search box was the worst caller of it

`search(query)` called `expandAll()` to put every row in the document and then hid the non-matches.
So a question about a handful of nodes rendered the entire tree — and the input is wired to
`oninput`, so it did that per keystroke.

**UI-016 made this actively worse before this fixed it.** Giving `expandAll` an accurate count meant
its confirm prompt started firing correctly, and `search` calls `expandAll` — so after §20, typing
one character into the box popped a modal on any trace over 400 nodes. A correct fix to one function
became a user-facing defect in another, because the caller was reaching for "materialise
everything". That is the strongest argument in this registry for fixing the *caller* rather than
making the expensive operation cheaper.

Matches are now found in the tree data and only the ancestor paths of matches are rendered. Results
are unchanged: the search compares the same two strings the row displays — the qualified name in
`.ct-name` and the owner schema in `.ct-schema-badge` — and a test asserts both still match, because
narrowing what a search box finds is the kind of change nobody notices until they cannot find
something.

**Not moved server-side, which is what the row asked for.** With the substring decision recorded in
§22 there is no server-side statement search to move to, and the tree the client holds is already
bounded by what the server sent. The row's intent — *typing does not materialise the tree* — is met.

### The gap I found in my own fix

Capping the matches bounds what is **rendered**. It does not bound the **walk**: a query matching
nothing still visits every node, and while someone is typing "matches nothing" is the common case.
So the slowest possible answer would have been the most frequent one, on the largest possible tree,
per keystroke. `MAX_SEARCH_SCAN: 50000` bounds the walk too, and the notice distinguishes "showing
the first 200 matches" from "searched the first 50,000 calls and stopped" — two different facts that
one message would have blurred.

Found by writing a test that failed for the wrong reason: the harness stores `innerHTML` as a string
rather than building retrievable elements, so nothing was rendered and my assertion tripped on a
limit of the harness. Chasing that surfaced the real gap.


## 25. Three middle-layer rows, none of which needed code

Worked through the remaining `MID-*` rows that looked unblocked. All three turned out to be
measurement or reading problems rather than implementation.

### MID-012 — satisfied by design; deleting the readers would break the only offline path

The row says to delete the N-file full-scan readers, DoD "no request reads every node file". The
scan is real and worth respecting: **64 node files, 5.42 MB per analysis**, which at the 8,000-
procedure target is ~8,000 files and roughly 680 MB.

But it does not happen per request. `MongoAnalysisRepository.document` takes the scan **once**, on
the first touch of an analysis, writes the result into the `facets` collection, and every request
after that is a single indexed `find` on `(runId, table)`. The readers the row names are that
seeding pass plus `ArtifactScanRepository`, which is the implementation for running with no
database at all. Deleting them would remove the offline mode and the seeding path together.

Marked ☑ against the DoD as written, with the mechanism recorded, because the alternative is
someone eventually "completing" it by deleting the two things that make it work.

### MID-009 — withdrawn on a measurement already in this document

`/source/{file}` reads one file with `readAllBytes`. Largest measured: **94.3 KB**. A procedure's
source does not grow with the corpus — the *number* of procedures does, and each request asks for
one. §12 already recorded this; the row was never updated to match. Withdrawn rather than left
open, so the list stops implying there is work here.

### MID-002 — the server half is ready and the client half would be churn

Measured: `nodes[]` is **84.1% of a 148.4 KB `/index` response** (114 nodes), and it scales with
procedure count. `/procedures` already exists, paged and faceted. `PA.analysisData.nodes` is now
read in **one** file — `nodeIndex.js` — which is exactly the seam that file was created to provide,
and its own doc comment says so.

So the server change is a two-line strip of the response, and safe: `getProcedures` reads `nodes`
out of the *artifact*, not out of the HTTP response.

**The client half is where it stops.** `_renderLeftProcedures` renders the full list synchronously
and filters it client-side, so moving the array from `/index` to `/procedures` would ship the same
bytes in one more request. The benefit only arrives when the sidebar itself stops needing every row
— which is the filter-behaviour decision recorded in this section's Decisions block
(threshold-based is the recommendation). Doing the strip now would be motion without effect, and
would leave the codebase mid-change with no test able to tell the difference.

**Row left ◐ with the blocker corrected** from `MID-001` (done) to the sidebar decision, which is
the thing actually in the way.


## 26. MID-010 already true, MID-015 gated rather than deleted

### MID-010

`/analyses` is already paged with a `page` envelope, and `/analyses/facets` answers counts and
dropdown values from the unfiltered set. Its "N-file scan" is one `index.json` read per analysis on
the list — the list *is* the set of analyses, so reading one file per row is what the question means,
not a defect the row can remove. The call site already says so: *"One index.json read per analysis,
which is inherent to the list."* Nothing to build; the row described work that was never separable
from the feature.

### MID-015

`GET /{id}` (JAR analyses) streams the entire document — a real one reaches 912 MB — and even the
streaming still passes through `classes` and `endpoints`, most of the bytes. Checked across every
`.js` file under `jar/`: **nothing calls it.** `getAnalysis()` in `jar/js/api.js` has zero callers.
Every screen moved to `/summary/header`, `/summary/endpoints` and the rest some time ago, matching
the same "declared but never wired" shape as `am_txn_statement` and `IdCodec.dbColumn` — except here
it is an entire endpoint, not a field.

**Not deleted.** A script outside this repository may still call it, and nothing inside the repo can
tell. Gated instead: the default request gets a 410 naming the three narrower replacements, and
`?full=true` is kept as an explicit, loud escape hatch — MID-004's pattern for `/call-graph`, applied
here for the first time as actual code (§15 recorded that MID-004 itself left the old route un-410'd).

Tested with a 21-argument constructor built by reflection rather than by hand, since only
`ObjectMapper` is exercised — the gated path returns before any of the other twenty collaborators are
touched, and a hand-written mock list would need updating every time the controller grows an
unrelated dependency. Calibration: removing the gate errors all three body-shape assertions;
inverting it so `full=true` is also refused fails the one test that checks the escape hatch works.


## 27. MID-008 asks for the wrong precomputation

`am_facet_count` answers "how many SELECTs, per schema, per table, in this run" — computed once,
independent of any query, for a panel that opens constantly. `/search/summary`'s facets answer a
different question: "how many SELECTs **among the rows matching what was just typed**". The two
cannot be the same data. A `col:QTY` search narrows the facet counts to rows containing `QTY`;
`am_facet_count` has no `q` to narrow by, because it was computed before any query existed.

Wiring `/search/summary` to it would not make the facets faster — it would make them **wrong**:
every search would show the unfiltered totals regardless of what was typed. That is worse than the
`$group` the row wants to avoid, which is at least correct.

Checked while establishing this: **`am_facet_count` has no reader anywhere** — not a wrong one, none
at all, in `analyzer-storage` or `unified-web`. It is ingested (`FacetCounter`, verified by
`FacetCountTest`) for a serving path that does not exist yet. That is a fourth instance of "written,
never wired" in this registry, on a collection rather than a field or a method.

The row is left ◐ rather than closed, because the part it can deliver — bounding the memory cost of
serving `/search/summary` — is already done. MID-007's streaming fix applies to `/search/summary`
too: it calls the same `search()` method, so it inherited the fix without a separate change. What
remains, wiring an unfiltered facet panel to `am_facet_count`, is a different feature the row's
wording conflates with this one, and building it here would be inventing scope rather than closing
a row.


## 28. VER-005, and a rule that is documented but not built

The row asks for a proof that `RoundTripProver`'s exemption is exact: it treats `null` and empty
containers as legitimately absent, so the proof needs the boundary — a value one step outside the
exemption must still be caught, or the exemption is wider than it claims to be.

Written as a unit test on the pure function (`RoundTripProver.compare`), not through a database:
this is a property of comparison logic, and exercising it that way needs no fixture, no Mongo, and
runs in 0.13 s. Ten cases: three inside the exemption (null, empty object, empty array), two just
outside it (the same container non-empty), and three scalars that must never be treated as
omittable (empty string, zero, `false`) even though each looks "empty" in a different sense.

### The `false` case is not what the row's title implies

`RELATIONAL-MODEL-PLAN.md` §17.1 documents Rule 1 as "omit null/**false**/empty keys on write" and
measures a 24–26% byte saving from doing so. Reading the actual write path —
`Splitter.flatten` and `JsonDocs.toValue` — **neither omits a boolean `false`**: it is written like
any other scalar. The plan's measurement is real; the implementation it argues for is not there.

So the test proves today's actual behaviour — a dropped `false` field is a real loss and must be
reported — rather than the plan's aspiration. A corroborating test
(`theWritePathToday_doesNotActuallyOmitFalse`) calls `Splitter.flatten` directly and asserts the
`false` field survives, so if someone later implements the boolean clause, **that** test fails
first and points at the two boolean-omission tests that need the wire-format decision described in
`OmissionExactnessTest`'s own javadoc — not a silent "fix" by loosening an assertion.

**Why this is a decision and not a bug to close here.** Implementing Rule 1's boolean clause changes
the wire format for every boolean field in every collection: present-`false` becomes absent, and
every reader doing `doc.getBoolean(key)` or `doc.containsKey(key)` has to treat absence and `false`
as the same fact. That is a blast-radius change across the whole ingest module, not a one-line fix
to a comparison function, so it is recorded rather than made unilaterally — the same reasoning as
MID-007's search semantics.


## 29. P4/P5 close-out — three new mappers, one silently-dropped field, and a collection with no schema at all

Worked the remaining `ING-*`/`VER-*` rows one by one, per instruction. Three were genuine gaps —
not naming mismatches, not stale numbers — the first of that kind since the §17 audit.

### ING-116/117: three artifact files nothing had ever opened

`MongoIngestService.ingestJar` read exactly one file, and its own comment justified skipping the
321 per-endpoint directories. It said nothing about `bundled-jars.json`, `jar-dep-map.json`, or
`external-links.json` — three files sitting at the same analysis root, never opened by any mapper
in this module.

- **`bundled-jars.json` → `am_bundled_jar` + `am_bundled_jar_resource`.** 100 bundled dependencies.
  Embedded, the worst entry reaches 465,644 B; a resource file's content can itself run to ~200 KB,
  and a resource file *name* is exactly the data-keyed-map shape `Splitter`'s guard exists to catch.
  Split, worst remaining doc is 61,636 B — close to but not exactly the plan's "≤62 KB", worth
  recording as another instance of a stale number rather than silently matching it up.

  **Self-introduced bug, caught before it shipped:** the resource key was built with
  `IdCodec.of(collection, jarEntityKey, ordinal)`. `of()` escapes every argument, and
  `jarEntityKey` was already an escaped, joined key — so its own `~` separators came out doubled,
  as literal `\~`, in the stored key. `IdCodec.nested()` exists for exactly this case and its own
  javadoc says so; I used the wrong one and only found it by reading a stored document by hand.
  Now pinned by a dedicated test (`everyResourceKeyIsWellFormed_noDoubleEscaping`).

- **`jar-dep-map.json` → `am_jar_dependency`.** 303 (jar, class) edges. `RELATIONAL-MODEL-PLAN.md`
  recommends embedding this in `bundled_jar.dependsOn[]`; split anyway, for the reason this module
  has now recorded three times — the no-arrays invariant is structural, not a per-array judgement.

  **A genuine cross-artifact disagreement, not an ingest defect:** two of the 18 jars named in the
  dependency map — `flow-poc-1.0.0-SNAPSHOT.jar` and `jackson-datatype-jsr310-2.15.4.jar` — are not
  separately catalogued in `bundled-jars.json`. `OrphanCheckerTest` now records this as a second
  known upstream finding, pinned by exact count exactly as `ANA-004` is, so a future reconciliation
  of the two source files makes the test fail and say so rather than silently keep passing.

- **`analysis.json`'s `advice` array was silently dropped.** Not a third-party file — a field of
  the file already being read, on both JAR mappers. `DagAndEndpointMapper`'s field switch fell
  through to `default -> p.skipChildren()`, and `AnalysisJsonMapper` never named it either. Two
  rows lost on every ingest, with nothing anywhere reporting a loss — a skipped field is
  indistinguishable from an absent one, which is the same failure mode as an unchecked reference
  one stage earlier in the pipeline.

- **`external-links.json` left undone, deliberately.** Every analysis on disk has `resolved: []`
  and `ambiguous: []`. There is no populated example anywhere to verify a mapper's field mapping
  against, and guessing a schema with nothing to check it against is how a wrong shape ships
  looking correct. Same treatment as `ING-019`'s DDL gap: recorded as blocked on data, not built
  speculatively.

### VER-007: the gate found a collection with no schema at all

The gate's first run found four "violations" that were three real, principled exceptions and one
real gap:

- `am_sql_text` — content-addressed and deliberately shared across runs (73% of captured SQL is
  duplicated); a `runId` field would force one row per (text, run) pair, defeating the dedup.
- `am_counter`, `am_meta` — schema bookkeeping, not per-run analysis data.
- **`am_run_member` had no catalog spec at all.** 14,810 rows, created implicitly on first insert,
  no validator, **no index on `runRef` or `entityRef`** — so "which entities does this run touch"
  and "which runs has this entity appeared in", the two questions this join collection exists to
  answer, were both collection scans. Given a spec and two indexes now; `_id` was already
  `runRef~entityRef` so no separate uniqueness constraint was needed.

The other three are recorded as a documented exception list, the same discipline
`OrphanRefChecker.NULLABLE` already uses — a judgement stated with its reason, not silence.

### VER-003: left open, because "the baseline" does not name anything

The row asks for a `CountReconciler` against "source JSON + baselines" from "§3-§5" of some
document. Those sections of `RELATIONAL-MODEL-PLAN.md` are schema design — entity models, logical
schema — not a table of expected counts. There is nothing to reconcile against. Building a
generalised reconciliation framework here would mean inventing the target it is supposed to check
against, and this session already has ~15 per-collection count tests doing the concrete version of
what the row asks for. Left open rather than built speculatively.
