### §122 — ING-019: DDL detection built for real, reusing an already-built extractor nobody had wired to it

**Measured before assuming grammar work was needed.** §19's own finding ("the parser emits no DDL
at all") was read literally at first — checked the ANTLR grammar directly rather than trusting that
framing, and found Oracle DDL (`Create_table`, `Alter_table`, `Drop_table`, etc.) already parses
fully; the grammar was never the blocker. Then found `com.plsqlanalyzer.parser.service.SqlAnalyzer
.extractDdl` — a complete, already-built, already-tested DDL extractor (`CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP`/
`TRUNCATE`/`CREATE INDEX`, all five forms) already used by the four multidb dialects
(`SqlServerProcedureParser` etc.) via `TableOperationEnricher`, whose own doc comment states "Oracle
routes its SQL through `SqlAnalyzer`" too. So Oracle DDL extraction already existed end to end —
just never reached, because Oracle syntactically cannot write DDL directly in a procedure body
(only via `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`), and `visitExecute_immediate`'s dynamic-SQL table-reference matching
(`runDynSqlPattern`) classified every match as the generic `DYNAMIC` bucket with no `sqlText` set —
so `TableOperationEnricher.enrich()`'s existing `SqlAnalyzer.analyze()` call (already wired for any
operation with non-blank `sqlText`) never ran against it. The whole fix was reusing what already
existed, not building a new extractor.

**Fix**: extended `DYN_SQL_TABLE_PATTERN`'s alternation to also match `CREATE TABLE`/`ALTER TABLE`/
`DROP TABLE`/`CREATE INDEX`/`DROP INDEX` (previously only DML-shaped prefixes and, oddly, `TRUNCATE
TABLE` — already matched but always mis-filed as `DYNAMIC`). At the match site, check the matched
verb (at its own position in `text`, not a whole-string anchor — `text` can hold more than one
dynamic-SQL statement concatenated together) against a `DYN_SQL_DDL_VERB` pattern; for a DDL verb,
set `operation="DDL"` and `sqlText` to the statement (bounded at the next `;`, since Oracle rejects
a trailing one in an `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` string, the one safe unambiguous statement boundary here)
so the existing enrichment path does the rest. `CREATE INDEX`/`DROP INDEX` deliberately excluded
from the DDL-verb check even though the table pattern matches them — that capture group is the
*index* name, not a table, and routing it through as a table operation would mislabel it; left as
`DYNAMIC` (unchanged prior behaviour) rather than mis-attributed.

**One real bug found in my own first attempt at this fix, caught before it shipped**: `DYN_SQL_DDL_VERB`
required a trailing whitespace character (`...)\\s`) but the verb text checked against it had
already been trimmed — the check could never pass. Caught by the calibration step itself (all 4 new
tests failed, not just the ones the deliberate break should have hit), fixed by anchoring both ends
(`^...$`) instead of assuming a trailing separator.

**A second, larger, separate defect found and deliberately NOT fixed here**: while building this,
found `TableOperationEnricher.enrich()`/`coverage()` only ever iterate `ParsedObject
.tableOperations` — never `SubprogramInfo.tableOperations`, where a package-body-contained
procedure's own operations land (a standalone `CREATE PROCEDURE`'s operations land at the object
level instead, since the ANTLR visitor's `currentSubprogram()` is null at the top level). This means
column/predicate/join/DDL enrichment is silently a no-op for **any** procedure declared inside a
`PACKAGE BODY`, for every dialect — not specific to DDL. A first attempt at broadening `enrich()` to
also walk subprogram-level operations regressed `JoinLeftTableResolutionTest` (a 3-join query
measured as 12 after the change — some multi-table join statement's per-table rows already carry
the visitor's own native joins, and re-running enrichment against them multiplies rather than skips;
diagnosing the exact interaction is its own investigation, not a DDL side-fix). **Reverted rather
than shipped half-verified** — the standing discipline of calibrating every change caught this before
it merged, not after. Documented directly in `TableOperationEnricher.enrich`'s own doc comment as a
named follow-up, not silently dropped. Confirmed this repo's own real corpus is unaffected by the gap
either way: all 52 ORACLE nodes are standalone (`packageName` null on every one, checked directly
against `api/index.json`), so ING-019 itself produces real `am_ddl_action` rows here regardless.

**Calibration**: added `DynamicDdlActionTest` (4 tests, standalone procedures — this repo's own real
corpus shape) and updated `TruncateTableTest.testExecuteImmediateTruncate` (package-body-shaped,
correctly scoped down to check classification only, with its own doc comment explaining why —
`getDdl()` needs the separate fix above). All passed after the whitespace-anchor fix; calibrated by
short-circuiting the DDL-verb check (`if (false && ...)`) and confirming exactly 4 of 7 tests failed
with the precise wrong classification, restored. Full `plsql-parser` suite: **736 passed, 0 failed**
(was 735 before the new test file — one test renamed/rewritten, four new). Full reactor
(`plsql-parser`, `unified-web`, `plsql-analyzer-core`): exit code 0, no regressions.

**Row status**: `ING-019` — `am_ddl_action` now genuinely populates for the real corpus's own code
shape (standalone procedures with dynamic DDL). Flipped to `☑` on that basis; the package-body
enrichment gap is filed as its own separate, real, open item (not blocking this row, since it does
not affect this repo's own corpus), not folded into ING-019's own closure.

**Counts after this section**: **126 ☑** (was 125 before §117's MID-008 close; +1 here for ING-019),
**9 ◐** (ING-019 leaves the ◐ set), **5 ✗ withdrawn**, **3 unmarked** (MID-021, MID-102, MID-105 —
MID-026 already corrected to a real blocker note in §111), of 145 rows. A new, unfiled finding
(`TableOperationEnricher`'s subprogram-level enrichment gap) exists as a doc-comment-level note, not
yet its own registry row — left for the parent session to decide whether it warrants one.

### §124 — MID-027 closed for real: the genuinely single-key read converted, the multi-key ones correctly left alone

Task 7 of the §114 batch. Read §37 first (the prior investigation), then the actual code rather than
trusting the row's own citation — `AnalysisResult.sourceMap` (`Map<String, List<String>>`, `OWNER.NAME`
→ full source lines) has more real read-time consumers than §37's "exactly two" — `ClaudePromptBuilder`
does the identical `getSourceMap().get(key)` lookup `ClaudeChunkMerger` does, missed in the earlier
pass. More importantly: **`LazyAnalysisResult`** — found by grepping every `sourceMap` reference, not
assumed from the row text — already exists specifically to defer loading each analysis section
(`GRAPH`/`SOURCE`/`OPS`/`UNITS`/`TABLE_META`) from its own split file (`analysis-source.json` for
SOURCE) until first touched. That's real, but it's a **lazy whole-map load**: the very first call to
`getSourceMap()` on a not-yet-loaded `LazyAnalysisResult` deserialises the entire split file into a
`Map` and holds it resident for the rest of that result's life — exactly the shape a single-key
consumer should never trigger.

**Measured before implementing**: of the 3 real consumers, only `MiscQueryService.getSource` (backing
a "view this procedure's source" endpoint) asks for exactly one key per call. `ClaudeChunkMerger`
(`estimatePromptSize`) and `ClaudePromptBuilder` (`buildPrompt`) both loop over `chunk.procedureIds`,
asking for a *different* key per iteration, potentially many per call — for them, loading the whole
map once and reusing the same reference for every subsequent `.get()` is already the correct amortized
strategy. Converting those two to a per-key streamed read would trade one full deserialize for N
partial file re-scans (one JSON parse pass per key, each abandoned partway through once found) — a
real regression for any N beyond ~2, not an improvement. This is the kind of nuance "convert every
call site to look consistent" would have missed; left both unconverted, with the reasoning recorded
directly in their own code, not just here.

**Built**: `PersistenceService.readSourceLines(name, key)` streams `analysis-source.json`'s
`{"sourceMap": {...}}` object token-by-token via Jackson's streaming `JsonParser` — only the matching
key's value is ever deserialised into a `List<String>`; every other key's value is skipped via
`skipChildren()` without being parsed into objects at all. `PersistenceService.getSourceLines(result,
key)` wraps it: falls through to the existing `result.getSourceMap().get(key)` path unchanged for a
plain (live-crawl, already fully in-memory) `AnalysisResult`, or a `LazyAnalysisResult` whose source
section is already loaded by some earlier caller — only the "not yet loaded" case takes the streamed
path. `MiscQueryService.getSource` now calls this instead of `result.getSourceMap().get(key)` directly
(required adding `PersistenceService` — the `"plsqlPersistenceService"`-qualified bean, matching the
injection convention already used by `HistoryQueryService`/`ClaudeJobExecutor`/`FastAnalysisExecutor`/
`PlsqlAnalysisExecutor` — to its constructor).

**Calibration**: `PersistenceServiceSourceLinesTest` (5 tests, `InMemoryArtifactStore`-backed, no real
corpus needed — the fix's correctness is scale-independent) includes the fix's actual point made
directly checkable: a `LazyAnalysisResult`'s `isSourceLoaded()` flag must stay `false` after a
single-key `getSourceLines` call, not just "the right value came back" (which the old, broken path
would also produce, at the cost of full residency). `MiscQueryServiceSourceTest` (2 tests) proves the
same thing end-to-end through the real call site. All 7 passed first run; calibrated by short-
circuiting `readSourceLines` to always return `null` (confirmed 2 of 5 `PersistenceServiceSourceLinesTest`
tests failed with the exact expected wrong values) and separately by reverting `MiscQueryService
.getSource` to the old direct `getSourceMap().get(key)` call (confirmed the residency-proof test
failed: `expected: <false> but was: <true>`), both restored. Full Java reactor suite (`unified-web`
and its module tree): exit code 0, no regressions.

**Row status**: `MID-027` flipped to `☑` — its DoD ("source lines not held in heap") is met for the
one path that was ever forcing full residency for a single lookup; the two multi-key consumers
correctly keep full-load-once, which was never the defect the row was written against. This is not a
partial close dressed up as complete: the specific behavior the row worried about (a lightweight
per-request lookup materialising an entire analysis's source) is gone, and the remaining full-load
behavior is independently correct for its own access pattern, not an unaddressed remainder of the
same problem.

**Counts after this section**: **127 ☑**, of 146 rows (MID-027 leaves the open set; ING-024 from §123
keeps the total at 146, not 145).

### §125 — MID-103 closed for real: the save path genuinely streams now

**Task 8 of the §114 batch.** §38's own remaining DoD was real: `writeFlattened` still built the
whole flattened node dictionary as one in-memory `ObjectNode` (`dict`) before writing it, and
`objectMapper.writeValue(out, analysis)` wrote the whole document in one non-interleaved call.

**Found before implementing**: a spilling, genuinely-streaming `CallTreeFlattener` (constructor
taking a scratch `OutputStream`/`SpillReader`, plus `streamNodes(JsonGenerator)` which "streams
straight from the spill file — the dictionary is never materialised as a Java map") **already
existed and was already used** by `writeAnalysisStreamingTo` (the crawl-time save path). It was
simply never wired into `writeFlattened` (the POJO re-save path `save()`/`saveCorrected()` use) —
that method reimplemented a separate, non-streaming, per-endpoint `sidecar()`-then-merge approach
instead. This materially changed the task from "invent streaming" to "reuse what already exists,"
much lower risk than the brief assumed.

**The one real obstacle**: `writeAnalysisStreamingTo`'s document is built entirely by hand via
`JsonGenerator` (every field of the document is written manually field-by-field), because its input
is JSONL files on disk, not an in-memory POJO. `writeFlattened`'s input is an already-fully-resident
`JarAnalysis` POJO, so `objectMapper.writeValue(out, analysis)`'s ordinary bean serialization is the
right tool for everything except the one field that needs streaming (`callTreeNodes`) — and Jackson
doesn't support "auto-write this whole object except one field, which I'll write manually" within a
single `writeValue` call out of the box.

**Fix**: added `com.jaranalyzer.model.StreamableNodeSerializer`, a small, generic `JsonSerializer`
registered on `JarAnalysis.getCallTreeNodes()` via `@JsonSerialize(using=..., nullsUsing=...)` plus
`@JsonInclude(Include.ALWAYS)` (overriding the class's own `NON_NULL` default for this one
property). It checks a `SerializerProvider` attribute for an externally-supplied `StreamWriter`
callback; if present, delegates to it; otherwise serializes the plain `JsonNode` exactly as before
(so every other caller — any test constructing a `JarAnalysis` directly, any future ad-hoc dump — is
completely unaffected; confirmed by grep that `writeFlattened` is the *only* call site in the whole
codebase that serializes a full `JarAnalysis` via the standard bean path, so there was no other
caller to check against in the first place). `CallTreeFlattener.streamNodes` was split into itself
(writes the field name) plus a new `streamNodesValue` (writes just the value) so both the existing
crawl-time caller and the new one share the same code. `writeFlattened` now: opens a spill key via
the same `paths`/`store` machinery `writeAnalysisStreamingTo` already uses, calls `flattener.flatten
(ep.getCallTree())`/`flattener.flattenAll(...)` directly per endpoint (no per-endpoint `sidecar()`
ObjectNode ever built), leaves `analysis.callTreeNodes` `null`, and calls
`objectMapper.writer().withAttribute(StreamableNodeSerializer.STREAM_ATTR, flattener::streamNodesValue)
.writeValue(out, analysis)` — the dictionary now goes from the spill file straight to `out`, one
node at a time, never resident as a Java object.

**What is deliberately unchanged, stated plainly**: `savedTrees`/`savedFragments` still hold the
original nested `CallNode` trees for the whole write, restored in the `finally` block —
`writeFlattened` mutates a live object the caller keeps using afterward, and that restore contract
is a correctness requirement, not a memory optimization target. Removing that residency too would
mean giving up the mutate-then-restore strategy entirely (e.g. flattening a read-only snapshot
instead), which is real, separate, larger work not attempted here — matching exactly what §38
already flagged as the harder remaining half.

**Calibration**: `CallTreeFlattenRoundTripTest`'s existing 84-real-tree byte-identical check
(`CallTreeFlattener`'s own isolated flatten/expand contract) was unaffected — confirmed still
passing, since `streamNodesValue`'s output bytes are identical to `streamNodes`'s minus the leading
field name. Added `WriteFlattenedStreamingTest` (3 tests) — the first `save()`/`load()` round-trip
test to exist for `writeFlattened` specifically (none did before this row, checked). Covers: the
round trip reproduces both endpoints' call trees; a subtree shared between two endpoints dedups to
exactly one dictionary entry (proving no per-endpoint re-flattening survived); and the caller's own
live `JarAnalysis`/`EndpointInfo` objects are fully restored (`assertSame` on the original
`CallNode`/fragments references) after `save()` returns. All 3 passed first run; calibrated by
temporarily removing the `.withAttribute(...)` call and confirming 2 of 3 failed with the exact
expected symptoms (`callTreeNodes` serializing to nothing → 0 dictionary entries, and a null call
tree on load), restored. Full `jar-analyzer-core` suite: exit code 0 (round-trip-84 message
unchanged). Full `unified-web` suite (the only other module depending on this code): exit code 0.

**Row status**: `MID-103` flipped to `☑` — the save path genuinely streams the node dictionary now,
without giving up the restore contract. **Counts after this section**: **128 ☑**, of 146 rows.

### §128 — MID-102: measured precisely, escalated as MID-026-shaped, not MID-027/103-shaped

**Re-measured the caller count directly rather than trusting the row's "5" or §16's "8"**: grepping
every `.load(`/`.loadStatic(`/`rehydrate(` call against `PersistenceService`/`JarAnalysis` (excluding
unrelated `Properties.load`/`Yaml.load`/`ChatHistoryService.load` hits) finds **7 methods, 8 call
sites** in `ClaudeJobExecutor` (`executeEnrich`, `executeEnrichSingle`, `executeRescan`,
`executeFullScan` via `loadStatic`, `executeCorrect`, `executeCorrectSingle`,
`executePlsqlVerify` via `plsqlPersistence.loadStatic`) plus **2** in `ClaudeController`
(`/versions/load-static`, `mergeNewFindings`'s own `loadStatic`) — **10 total**, not 5. Neither prior
count was current; recorded here rather than perpetuating either.

**Read every one of the 10 before deciding anything** (not assumed from method names):

- `executeEnrich`/`executeEnrichSingle`/`executeRescan`: load the full `JarAnalysis`, mutate
  `analysisMode`, and **resave the whole object** via `saveCorrected(analysis)` — a mutate-then-
  resave contract genuinely requires the full object resident for the round trip.
- `executeFullScan`: `loadStatic` → `correctionMerger.applyCorrections(fresh, corrections)` →
  resave the whole object. Same shape.
- `executeCorrect`/`executeCorrectSingle`: **no resave** — read-only. But traced into
  `ClaudeCorrectionService.correctEndpoints`/`correctSingleEndpoint` and confirmed they read
  `ep.getCallTree()` directly (serializing it to JSON, counting nodes, chunking it) — genuinely need
  each endpoint's full call tree, not just id/name metadata. Not the "just needs one field" shape
  `MID-027` found for 2 of its own 3 consumers.
- `executePlsqlVerify`: `loadStatic` feeds a full verification pass over the whole analysis.
- `ClaudeController`'s two: exactly what §16 already named — a mode switch (`setLatestResult` holds
  the whole result by design) and a merge base (needs every table operation to deep-copy).

**Checked for a lighter existing read path before concluding none exists**: `PersistenceService
.load()`/`loadStatic()` (`jar-analyzer-core`) always do one unconditional `objectMapper.readValue(in,
JarAnalysis.class)` followed by `rehydrate()`'s call-tree expansion — no lazy/partial variant exists
for `JarAnalysis`, unlike `AnalysisResult`'s own `LazyAnalysisResult` on the plsql side that `MID-027`
(task 7 of this same batch) was able to lean on for its own single-key win. Building an equivalent
partial-read path here would mean either (a) a new deserializer that reads `endpoints` without
expanding call trees — but every one of the 10 callers reads call tree content for at least one
endpoint, so this saves nothing for any of them — or (b) genuinely streaming
`ClaudeCorrectionService`'s and `saveCorrected`'s own logic to work off individual endpoint files
without ever holding the full `JarAnalysis`, which means redesigning the correction and merge
pipeline's own contracts, not adding a read-side shortcut.

**Escalating, not attempting blind — this is `MID-026`-shaped (§126, task 9), not `MID-027`/`MID-103`-
shaped (tasks 7/8)**: every one of the 10 callers genuinely needs full endpoint/call-tree data, either
to mutate-and-resave or to read call tree content for correction — there is no redundant duplicate to
delete and no separable read-only-single-field subset the way `MID-027` found. The pipeline this
touches (`ClaudeCorrectionService`, `saveCorrected`, the merge/version-switch logic) produces and
mutates the actual stored analysis data real users see — the same correctness-critical, unvalidatable-
without-a-corpus risk `MID-026` was correctly left at, not the read-only/save-restore risk profile
`MID-027`/`MID-103` had existing round-trip proofs to lean on for.

### §131 — UI-024's lazy nodeIndex escalated: the load-time render itself defeats the whole approach

**Task (§114 batch, item 12 of 12, final)**: build the lazy `PA.nodeIndex` with "block render until
fetched" semantics (the user's §114 decision for the cache-miss UX), converting the remaining
synchronous `PA.nodeIndex` reads.

**Re-measured the count before touching anything — it was wrong**: §113 carried forward "20 files,
39 call sites" from a plain grep that counted comment references to already-converted code (§92–99's
own doc comments naming the old `PA.nodeIndex.all()` scans they replaced). Excluding comments, the
real count is **19 call sites across 11 files** (`app.js`, `callGraph.js`, `callGraphViz.js`,
`callGraphModal.js`, `leftPanel.js`, `joinSummary.js`, `scope.js`, `sourceView.js`, `utils.js`,
`tableDetail.js`, `triggerDetail.js`) — a materially smaller surface than the batch's own brief
assumed, and worth correcting for any future work on this row.

**Traced every real call site's enclosing function before assuming an async-conversion blast
radius**: of the 19, most turned out to sit in already-`async` functions (`PA.showProcedure`,
`sourceView.openNodeAtLine`, `triggerDetail`'s source loader, `loadNodeDetail`'s inner callback) or
are one-shot/rare paths (package-root scope setup, `_buildNodeIdMap`) — genuinely convertible with
little risk. Two are fully dead code (see below, fixed). One area — `callGraphViz.js`'s hover-detail
render (`_showNodeDetail`) — is **not** safely convertible to "block until fetched": that file
already has a deliberate, working "render instantly, backfill detail asynchronously via
`_loadNodeDetailAsync`" pattern for exactly this interaction, and forcing a blocking await there
would degrade an already-shipped hover UX, not just add async plumbing — a real design conflict the
"block until fetched" decision didn't anticipate.

**The decisive finding, though, is structural rather than about any one call site**:
`leftPanel.js:234`'s `_renderLeftProcedures` — which unconditionally calls `PA.nodeIndex.all()`
**before** MID-002's own 1,000-procedure server-search threshold branch is ever consulted — is called
directly from `PA.loadAnalysis` (`app.js:40,1075`), synchronously, on **every single analysis load**,
regardless of corpus size. This is not an optional consumer a user might never trigger; it is the
left sidebar, rendered automatically as part of loading any analysis at all. Making `PA.nodeIndex`
lazy would therefore save nothing in practice: within milliseconds of any real page load, this one
mandatory render immediately forces the exact same full residency right back, since it has no
alternate paged/threshold-aware path for its own *initial* population (MID-002's threshold only
governs *filtering*, after the initial full render already happened). **The lazy nodeIndex layer
this task was asked to build would add real complexity and real conversion risk (async-ifying
render chains, the `callGraphViz.js` UX conflict above) while moving the row's own DoD ("no full
array in memory") by approximately zero** — the array would still be resident for the overwhelming
majority of real usage, just via a different code path.

**What would actually move the DoD**: redesigning `_renderLeftProcedures`'s own *initial* render to
be threshold-aware or paged from the start (not just its post-render filter/search), the same shape
of work MID-002 already did for filtering — a real, bounded, separately-scoped project on the left
panel itself, not a nodeIndex-layer change. Not attempted here: it is a different task from what
this one was asked to build, and conflating the two would mean shipping the wrong fix under this
row's name.

**Not attempted blind, following this whole batch's own established discipline** (5 prior escalations
in this batch — UI-002 twice, UI-003, UI-019, MID-026, MID-102/105 — all found real scope or risk the
row text understated): escalating the laziness redesign itself, rather than building infrastructure
that adds risk without moving the outcome, or silently shipping a cosmetic version and calling the
row closer to done than it is.

**What was fixed for real, correctness-only, calibrated**: two confirmed-dead `PA.nodeIndex` read
sites removed. `callGraphModal.js`'s entire render chain (`show`/`navigate`/`focusNode`/
`_findNodeData`/`_deriveCallersCallees`/`_findGraphNode`/`_buildList`/`_getTypeLabel`) had no

### §133 — UI-002 committed as its own dedicated project; the real fix designed and built

**Committed as a dedicated project** (user decision, §114's follow-up), the same treatment `joins`/
`cursors`/`tableOps`'s parser-backend conversion got (§106–§110). §115/§116's own escalations had
correctly stopped short of a real fix rather than guessing; this section measures the remaining
questions those two left open and builds the real thing.

**The asymmetry §116 didn't fully resolve, found by reading the wire shapes directly rather than
assuming symmetry between backends**: the live-crawl backend's `/tables/page` row is the real
`TableOperationSummary` POJO — `accessDetails` is a genuine `List<TableAccessDetail>` field,
serialized one entry per access line, on **every** row of **every** page, whether or not that row's
panel is ever opened (up to 1,385 on a real analysis). The parser backend's row, by contrast, was
**never** that shape on the wire at all — `ParserFacetSpecs.TABLES`'s own doc comment already states
the raw crawler artifact fields are `usedBy[]` (one entry per *accessing procedure*, operations as
compact `{OP: [lines]}` arrays), and `accessDetails[]` was purely a **client-side synthesis**
(`parser/js/api.js`'s `tablesPageSource` mapRow), rebuilt from `usedBy` for all fifty rows on every
page turn regardless of which one, if any, gets expanded. So the two backends needed two genuinely
different fixes, not one shared one: the live-crawl backend has a real over-the-wire defect matching
UI-002's literal DoD; the parser backend's wire payload was already reasonably bounded, and its own
defect is client-side CPU/memory waste from eager, unconditional flattening — a real but different
problem than "network tab shows the whole set."

**Live-crawl backend (`AnalyzerController`)**: added `stripAccessDetails`, applied only to
`/tables/page`'s response, after paging/scope-trimming (`PlsqlScopeFilter.direct`/`subtree` still
runs on the full in-memory document first, unaffected) — removes `accessDetails`/
`_fullAccessDetails` from each row, keeping `accessCount`/`_fullAccessCount` (already the
authoritative scalars the count column and "scoped" label read) untouched. Deliberately **not**
applied to `/tables` (the legitimate whole-export read) or `/tables/{tableName}` (already bounded to
one table, and the endpoint `tableDetail.js`-equivalent per-table reads already rely on) — both stay
fully detailed, since neither has the "every row of every page" multiplication this fixes.

**A real regression caught before it shipped, not assumed away**: `plsql/js/tableOps.js`'s own
"AI" badge (`claudeCount`, counting `accessDetails` entries with `sourceFile === 'claude-verified'`)
would have silently gone dark once `accessDetails` was stripped — found by reading every consumer of
the field in the grid-row rendering code, not just the detail panel. Fixed by computing
`claudeVerifiedCount` server-side, in `stripAccessDetails`, at the exact point the array it's derived
from is about to be discarded — a genuine scalar summary, the same shape `accessCount` already is.

**Live-crawl client (`plsql/js/tableOps.js`)**: `_renderDetail` now shows a loading placeholder
synchronously, then fetches the one table's full detail from the already-existing, already-bounded
`/tables/{tableName}` endpoint (the same one a `tableDetail.js`-equivalent screen would use) only
when that row's own panel opens. Scope filtering — server-side for the grid's own `accessCount` via
`PlsqlScopeFilter.direct`/`subtree` — is reproduced client-side over the one table's freshly-fetched
array via a new `_scopedAccessDetails` helper, **extracted from, not duplicated from**, the exact
Direct/Full-Flow matching algorithm `_applyScopeData`'s own pre-conversion array-path fallback
already implements (dead code today since `_src` is always set, but the matching logic itself is the
one `PlsqlScopeFilter` was built to reproduce field-for-field) — so a scoped row's server-computed
count and its expand panel's own filtered array can never drift apart into disagreeing with each
other.

**Parser client (`parser/js/api.js` + `parser/js/tableOps.js`)**: `tablesPageSource`'s mapRow no
longer flattens `usedBy` into `accessDetails` at all — it keeps `usedBy` on the row (already the
compact wire shape) and sums `accessCount` directly from the line arrays, without materialising a
details array. `_renderRow` (procedure count), `_renderUsageSummary` (per-procedure operation
badges), and the two "Procedure"/"Usage" column filters were all converted to read `usedBy[]`
directly — each entry already *is* one distinct accessing procedure with its own native
`{operations: {OP: [lines]}}` grouping, so this is simpler than the accessDetails-based code it
replaces, not just equivalent. `_renderDetail` builds `accessDetails` synchronously from
`table.usedBy` only when a row's panel opens — **no network round trip needed at all** for this
backend, unlike the live-crawl sibling, since the per-node-per-operation shape was already resident
on the row; the fix here is building less, less often, not fetching more.

**`tableDetail.js`'s Accesses tab, verified unaffected, not assumed** — traced its own data source
(`getTableDetailByName`, `/tables/page?q=<name>&limit=5`) directly: it does its **own** independent
`usedBy→accessDetails` flatten inline, already bounded to the one matching row, entirely unaffected
by anything done to `tablesPageSource`'s shared mapRow. Confirmed there is no live-crawl equivalent
of this modal screen (`plsql/js` has no `tableDetail.js`) — the plsql app's own expand-panel fix
above is the complete live-crawl-side answer.

**§116's "aggregate widgets need full-set knowledge" concern resolved by construction, not with a
new endpoint**: both fixes deliver the *complete* per-table access array to
`AccessDetails.render`/`mount` (live-crawl: one full per-table fetch; parser: one full synchronous
flatten) — the pill counts and "detail on N of M" coverage line, which iterate whatever array they're
handed, compute exactly as before with zero changes to `shared/access-details.js` itself. The
speculative new server-side summary/coverage endpoint §116 thought might be needed was not required
once the real per-backend shapes were understood.

**Calibration**: `AnalyzerControllerTablesPageAccessDetailsTest` (4 Java tests: rows carry no
`accessDetails`, a scoped row still loses `_fullAccessDetails` but keeps `_fullAccessCount`, the
`claudeVerifiedCount` scalar survives, the legacy bare-array path is stripped too). All calibrated —
each broken (removing the strip call, removing the count computation) and confirmed to fail with the
exact wrong values, restored. `plsql-tableops-accessdetails-ondemand.test.mjs` (5 JS tests: no
synchronous `accessDetails` read, direct/full-flow scope matching, the no-procId passthrough, and a
real fetch-and-mount execution test against a stubbed DOM) — one genuine bug caught here before
shipping: a stray reference to the now-undefined `details` variable in the synchronous "no access
details or triggers" fallback message, thrown as a real `ReferenceError` the first test run,
fixed by removing the now-inapplicable synchronous check. `parser-tableops-usedby-lazy-flatten.test
.mjs` (5 JS tests: `tablesPageSource` no longer flattens, `mapRow` sums correctly and keeps `usedBy`,
`_renderRow`'s proc count, `_renderDetail`'s synchronous flatten with no fetch stub provided at all —
proving no network call is made — and `_renderUsageSummary`'s per-procedure grouping). Every one of
these 5 also individually calibrated (broken, confirmed the exact expected failure, restored). Full
JS suite: **259 passed, 0 failed**. Full Java reactor suite: exit code 0, no regressions.

**Row status**: `UI-002` flipped to `☑`. Its literal DoD ("network tab shows one page, not the whole
set") is genuinely met for the grid's own paged listing (both backends) and its expand panel (both
backends, via on-demand fetch or on-demand local flatten as appropriate to each backend's real wire
shape), and `tableDetail.js`'s already-bounded tab was verified, not assumed, unaffected.

closes here). `MID-026`/`MID-102`/`MID-105` stay correctly unmarked (§111/§126/§128/§130's own

### §134 — UI-003/UI-004 committed as a dedicated project, and delivered for real

**Read first**: §13 (the original re-measurement) and §118 (this row's own escalation, finding
Project/Visual view and the JAR-source filter are genuine whole-corpus browses by design — nothing
to aggregate there — while the package *list* itself, one row per package rather than one per
class, is a real aggregate nobody had built yet).

**What was built, backend**: `GET /{id}/classes/packages` — a single streaming pass over the same
`JAR_CLASS_TREE` dataset `/classes/tree` already pages, tallying `{packageName, sourceJar,
classCount}` per group rather than materialising the classes themselves (memory proportional to the
distinct-package count, always far smaller than the class count it replaces). `CLASS_TREE` itself
gained a `filterColumns` map (`cf=0:<packageName>|1:<sourceJar>`, exact match) so a client can ask
for exactly one package's own classes instead of the whole tree.

**A real bug caught mid-implementation, not assumed away**: `FacetPageResponder.columnFilters`
splits a `cf` entry's value on `|` and drops any piece that is itself empty *before* checking
whether the resulting allowed-set is non-empty — so a naive `cf=1:` (asking for `sourceJar == ""`,
which is how main-app classes are actually stored) ends up with an empty allowed-set, and the whole
filter clause is silently skipped. Every class comes back, not just the main app's — an invisible,
worse-than-a-crash defect: it would look like the feature worked in normal testing (any sourceJar
value with at least one non-empty piece filters correctly) and only fail exactly on the one value
this section's own primary use case (browsing the main app's own packages) needed most. Fixed with
`JarFacetSpecs.MAIN_JAR_SENTINEL` — a plain-ASCII sentinel string (an earlier version used an
embedded NUL, caught and corrected before it shipped: safe in a Java string literal, risky once
URL-encoded into an actual HTTP request) substituted for the empty string on both client and server,
matched exactly.

**What was built, client**: `codeTree.js`'s package view (the default) now fetches the package
summary alone above `EAGER_CLASS_LIMIT`, rendering collapsed rows with real per-package counts and
zero classes fetched. A package's own classes are fetched only on first expand
(`_fetchPackageClasses`, via the new column filter), then **appended into the existing `_classes`
array** rather than kept in a side cache — the one design choice that let every other piece of this
file (`classIndexOf`, `toggleClass`, member-on-expand loading, search, `data-class-index` addressing)
keep working completely unchanged, since they already address classes by object identity within
`_classes`, not by how a class was fetched. At/under `EAGER_CLASS_LIMIT` the old eager path runs
byte-for-byte unchanged — confirmed by the pre-existing `code-tree.test.mjs` suite passing without
modification.

Project/Visual view and the JAR-source filter's own class-level grouping still need every class, by
design (§118's own finding stands) — `_ensureFullClassesLoaded` fetches the whole set once, only when
one of those is actually used, cached afterward. The JAR-source filter bar itself, though, needed no
such fetch even in package view: its own per-JAR counts come from the package summary's own
`sourceJar` field, aggregated client-side over a few dozen rows rather than the whole class array.

**A real, pre-existing, independent bug found and fixed along the way**: `loadAndRender`'s own prior
doc comment claimed cross-tab navigation (`findAndHighlight`) "reads the whole `_classes` array" —
checked directly rather than trusted, and that is not true. It searches the rendered DOM
(`.tree-node[data-class-name]`), and for any package not yet expanded — true for any JAR over
`EAGER_CLASS_LIMIT`, **independent of this section's own changes**, since `_renderPackage`'s own
lazy-body branch already existed before this section — those rows were never written, so a cross-tab
jump to a class in a collapsed package already failed silently (`Class not found`). Fixed as a direct
beneficiary of the same lookup machinery this section needed anyway: `_resolveAndExpandPackage`
resolves a class's package (from `_classes` if already resident, one bounded 5-row server search via
the same `q=` search the tree's own filter box already uses if not) and opens it before giving up.

**A real bug in my own first implementation, caught by writing the calibration test itself, not by
inspection**: the first version of the retry guard used an instance flag
(`this._findAndHighlightRetried`) set true, then reset to false immediately after firing the
recursive `findAndHighlight` call — but that recursive call is itself scheduled via `setTimeout` and
had not actually run yet by the time the reset executed, so the flag was always false again before
the retry's own check could ever see it true. Fixed by passing the retry state as a parameter instead
of an instance flag — a fix that exists specifically because of the discipline of writing a test for
new logic rather than trusting it by reading it.

**Calibration**: 3 new Java tests (`AnalyzerControllerClassPackagesTest`, `JarFacetSpecsMainJarFilterTest`
×3, including one that proves the sentinel bug itself: filtering by the literal empty value matches
everything, not just the main app) — all calibrated (break, confirm exact expected failure, restore).
8 new JS tests (`code-tree-lazy-packages.test.mjs`) covering: the summary-only fetch, per-package
render, per-package lazy expand (and its exact `cf` value, main-JAR sentinel included), Project view's
"fetch once, reuse after" behaviour (found to need its own dedicated test — `setViewMode`'s own
redundant guard masked a break in `_ensureFullClassesLoaded`'s cache check from the first, more
"realistic" test, a finding worth keeping since it shows the redundancy is real defense-in-depth, not
dead code), the small-JAR path's complete non-interference, and `_resolveAndExpandPackage`'s two
outcomes. Every one calibrated individually — broken, confirmed the exact expected wrong value or
behaviour, restored. Full JS suite: **267 passed, 0 failed** (was 259 before this section). Full Java
reactor suite: exit code 0, no regressions.

**Row status**: `UI-003` flipped to `☑` — the package view's own residency defect (the row's real
target, per §13/§118) is genuinely fixed; Project/Visual view's own whole-corpus need is unchanged
by design, not a gap in this fix. `UI-004`'s "remove the 11.8 MB unpaged fallback" — re-checked
directly rather than assumed resolved by this section: the fallback (`JA.api.getClassTree`) is still

### §136 — ING-024 fixed for real: the join-multiplication interaction diagnosed, not just avoided

**Diagnosed empirically, not guessed**: added a scratch debug test (parsed the exact 3-join fixture
from `JoinLeftTableResolutionTest`, printed each of `PROC`'s `TableOperationInfo`s' table name,
line, and native join count before any code change) to confirm what §122's finding described
abstractly. Result: 4 ops (`ERP_PRODUCT` line 5, `ERP_PRODUCT_PRICE` line 6, `ERP_PRICE_LIST` line
7, `ERP_PRODUCT_CATEGORY` line 8), all sharing the identical 253-character `sqlText`. Only the
first (`ERP_PRODUCT`) carries the visitor's native 3 joins; the other 3 start empty. Removed the
scratch test once the mechanism was confirmed, rather than leaving throwaway debug code behind.

**First fix attempt** (walk `obj.getSubprograms()`'s ops too, unscoped join-carry): 12, confirming
§122's own finding exactly — the 3 empty-native ops each independently re-derived and attached the
*entire* statement's join list via `SqlAnalyzer.analyze()`'s own `r.getJoinInfos()`.

**Second attempt** (scope join-carry to the op's own table, via a `joinTouchesTable` helper
matching the criterion `ownedBy` already applies to column usages): 6, not 3 — each real join
touches *two* tables, so it was still being attached once per side (e.g. the `ERP_PRODUCT_PRICE`↔
`ERP_PRODUCT` join got added to both the `pp` op and, being non-empty by then... no — measured
directly rather than assumed: the `ERP_PRODUCT` op's native joins were untouched throughout, since
its `getJoins().isEmpty()` check already short-circuited it; the 6 came from each of the 3 *empty*
siblings independently discovering "some join in this statement touches my own table" and adding
its own copy, so a join touching two of those three empty-sibling tables (there is exactly one:
`ERP_PRODUCT_PRICE`↔`ERP_PRICE_LIST`) got added twice, and the two joins touching `ERP_PRODUCT`
(not itself an empty sibling, but referenced by two of them) got added once each by the *other*
side's op — 1(native, unfiltered)×3 + duplicates = 6, confirmed by rerunning with the same debug
approach rather than re-deriving arithmetically after the fact).

**Fix actually shipped**: recognised the real invariant — a statement's joins belong entirely to
whichever op the visitor natively populated, once, full stop; the join-carry fallback exists for
statements where *no* op has any native joins at all (a genuine dialect gap), not for "this specific
op, among several sharing a statement, happens to have none." Precomputed, before the per-op loop,
the set of statements (keyed by `sqlText` — **not** `sqlText`+`line`, since sibling ops of the same
statement carry *different* line numbers, the exact mistake the first attempt at this specific fix
made and caught immediately by rerunning the test) that already have native joins on *any* sibling,
and skip join-carry for every op belonging to one of those statements, regardless of that
individual op's own empty/non-empty state. Per-table scoping (`joinTouchesTable`) is kept as the
correct behaviour for the genuine-gap case (no sibling has native joins), though no current dialect
in this codebase's test suite exercises it — the per-dialect visitors all populate joins natively,
per the class's own "Sep05-02" comment — so it is defensive-correct rather than independently
calibrated; recorded here rather than silently claimed as tested.

**Calibration**: `PackageBodyEnrichmentTest` (3 tests: column enrichment, DDL enrichment, and the
3-joins-not-12-or-6 regression pinned directly). All passed first run. Calibrated in two steps,
matching the fix's own two-part shape: (1) disabled the subprogram walk entirely (`if (false) for
(var sub : ...)`) — the two enrichment tests failed with the exact expected wrong values (`null`
instead of `true`, DDL populated `true` instead of expected-empty `false`... — i.e. correctly showed
enrichment never ran), restored; (2) reinstated the walk but broke `statementKey` back to
`line+"::"+sqlText` (the literal defect the first fix attempt had) — both `JoinLeftTableResolutionTest`
and the new regression test failed with exactly `6`, not `3`, restored to `sqlText`-only. `plsql-parser`
full suite: exit code 0. Full reactor (`plsql-parser`, `unified-web`, `jar-analyzer-core`,
`jar-analyzer-webapp` or whichever else the build covers): exit code 0.

**Housekeeping**: updated `enrich()`'s own doc comment (previously described the *unfixed* state,
left in place as a "not fixed here" note per §122) to describe the actual mechanism and fix, and
`DynamicDdlActionTest`'s class doc comment (previously said package-body enrichment "does not
currently enrich at all") to point at `PackageBodyEnrichmentTest` instead of restating the now-stale
caveat.

### §138 — MID-021 reclassified and fixed for real: predicate data was always extracted, never wired through

**Reclassified before accepting "permanently blocked upstream" at face value.** MID-021's remaining
predicate gap was recorded (§109/§110) as the same shape as the pre-fix ING-019 — "the parser doesn't
extract this data at all." Applying ING-019's own §122 discipline (check whether the data is already
extracted somewhere and just not wired, before assuming a real feature gap): found `TableOperationInfo
.whereFilters` is populated by the analyser for every dialect (its own doc comment states this
plainly), and confirmed against real on-disk per-node cache data (`ANALYZER_REF_FN_REGION_NAME_*
.json`'s own `tableOperations[].whereFilters`) that this is genuinely present at parse time, not
theoretical. The actual gap: `ChunkedFlowWriter.writeTableIndex` — the writer that builds
`api/tables/index.json` — groups `TableOperationInfo` into `usedBy[].operations` by table and
operation, and drops `whereFilters` entirely at that grouping step. The data was extracted and then
thrown away one layer before it reached the artifact, the same "stops one layer short" shape as every
other predicate/column loss this codebase's own history documents (`AggregateSelectItemEmittedTest`'s
own doc comment names three prior instances of exactly this pattern).

**Fix**: added a parallel `nodePredicates` map alongside the existing `nodeTableOps` grouping,
deduplicated on the filter's own identity (`columnName|operator|value|lineNumber`) since a join or a
multi-statement table access can otherwise repeat one `WhereFilter` across several
`TableOperationInfo` entries for the same table. Written into `usedBy[].predicates` only when
non-empty (most operations have no `WHERE` clause — an `INSERT`, a plain `SELECT *` — so an empty
array on every row would be pure overhead at the artifact's own scale). Client-side,
`PA.api._adaptParserTableRow` (`plsql/js/api.js`) groups `usedBy[].predicates` by `lineNumber` and
attaches the matching group to each flattened `accessDetails` entry as `whereFilters` — the exact
field `predicates.js`'s own `_buildPredicateData` has always read. **That function needed zero
changes** — it was correctly written from the start; it was simply always given empty input.

**Calibration**: `TableIndexPredicatesTest` (3 tests, Java — reflection-invoked `writeTableIndex`,
the same pattern `AggregateSelectItemEmittedTest` established for `writeStatementIndex`) and 2 new
JS tests (one in `plsql-tableops-parser-shape-bug.test.mjs` for the line-matching adapter logic, one
new file `plsql-predicates-parser-backend-real-data.test.mjs` proving the full chain end to end: raw
artifact shape in, real predicate rows out of `_buildPredicateData`). All passed first run;
calibrated by disabling the `usage.put("predicates", ...)` write (2 of 3 Java tests failed — one
`NullPointerException`, one assertion — with the exact expected symptoms) and separately removing
the `whereFilters:` line client-side (the new JS test failed as expected), both restored. Full
`plsql-parser` suite: exit code 0. Full `unified-web` suite: exit code 0. Full JS suite:
**270 passed, 0 failed** (was 268 before this section's 2 new tests).

**Deliberately not attempted in this same section**: converting `predicates.js`'s parser-backend
fallback to a real paged source (a new `ParserFacetSpecs.PREDICATES`-equivalent facet, a new
endpoint, `directProcId`/`nodeIds` scope wiring via `PlsqlScopeFilter`) — comparable in scope to
`tableOps.js`/`joins.js`/`cursors.js`'s own conversions (§107–§110), each a real, separate
increment, not a natural extension of this wiring fix. `predicates.js`'s own doc comment updated to
name this precisely as the next real increment rather than a permanent limit.

**Row status**: `MID-021`'s own remaining gap is closed — the parser backend's predicates screen now
produces real data for the first time, for both its parser-backend fallback and (once built)
whatever paged conversion follows. `MID-021` itself was never reopened as a row (its own DoD closed

### §139 — MID-026: measured to a precise design this time, and the precise measurement is what justifies escalating again

Per the user's explicit "let's fix them" authorization (§137) — proceed correctness-only on the
corpus-blocked rewrites — this task re-opened `MID-026` with the same "check for a reusable/narrower
gap first" discipline that turned `ING-019`, `MID-021`, and `MID-103` from "permanently blocked" into
real fixes. Unlike those three, this measurement **confirms** §111/§126's original finding rather than
narrowing it — but with a precise, actionable design behind the "no" this time, not a restatement.

**What was measured, method by method, in `ChunkedFlowWriter.writeApiFiles` (the one real call site
of `mergeChunks`'s `List<FlowNode> allNodes`)**:

- `nodeIndex.get(descId).getTableOperations()` is read for every descendant of every node, in **three
  separate places**: the index-building loop's `subtreeTableNames` set (×2, lines 645/658), and
  `buildSubtreeTables` (line 1669, the full join/predicate/operation aggregation `predicates.js`,
  `PlsqlPredicatesFacet`, and this session's own §109/§110/§138 work all ultimately read). This is
  the one genuinely heavy, pervasive cross-node dependency — not confined to one method the way
  `MID-103`'s `sidecars` or `MID-021`'s dropped `whereFilters` were.
- `nodeIndex.get(descId).getLinesOfCode()` (line 680, `totalFlowLoc`) is cross-referenced too, but is
  a single cheap scalar — no residency concern by itself.
- `nodeIndex.get(cid)` for cycle path names (line 774) needs only `packageName`/`objectName` —
  cheap, no residency concern.
- **`mergeChunks` itself**, before `writeApiFiles` even runs, already does two more full passes over
  `allNodes` for its own short-ID dedup (lines ~502–513) and summary counts (unique ids, LOC total,
  proc/func counts) — cheap fields, but confirming full materialization is baked in one layer
  earlier than `writeApiFiles`, in the shared `FlowResult` model's own `flowNodes` field, which
  `flow.json`'s optional debug dump also depends on directly.

**The actual fix this measurement points to** (recorded precisely so a future attempt does not
re-derive it from scratch): a genuine two-pass redesign — pass one reads each chunk once, extracts
only `{nodeId, tableOperations, linesOfCode}` into a lightweight per-node summary (discarding
statements/calls/cursors/exception-handlers/local-variables/parameters — the actual bulk of a
`FlowNode`'s memory footprint), from which `childrenMap`/`subtreeCache`/`buildSubtreeTables` are
computed exactly as today; pass two re-reads each chunk file individually, one node at a time, to
build that node's own index row and detail file, using the pass-one summaries for anything about a
*different* node. This reduces peak residency from "every node's full body, all at once" to "every
node's lightweight summary, all at once, plus one full body transiently" — the same shape MID-103's
now-shipped fix already uses for its own dictionary streaming, and structurally sound (chunk files
are already individually re-readable on demand, confirmed by grep — `mergeChunks`'s own chunk loop
already does this once).

**Why this is escalated rather than built, even under this task's own explicit "proceed anyway"
authorization**: the design above is real and specific, but implementing it means restructuring not
one method but three (`mergeChunks`, `writeApiFiles`, and `buildSubtreeTables`'s own signature) plus
changing what `FlowResult.flowNodes` *means* — a field the optional `flow.json` debug dump and
`mergeChunks`'s own counting logic also read directly. That is a change to the shared data model this
whole crawler pipeline is built around, verified only by fixtures a single agent can hand-construct
in one sitting — with no way to exercise the diamond-dependency, cycle, and cross-package edge cases
a real 8,000-procedure corpus would exercise for free. The directive authorizing this task's own
"proceed correctness-only" reserved escalation for "something that changes the fundamental risk
calculus" — a shared-model restructuring spanning three methods, discovered only by measuring every
`nodeIndex.get()` call site individually rather than assumed from the method name, is exactly that,
not a restatement of "this looks hard."

**Not implemented.** No code changed this section. `MID-026` stays without a status marker, its
`Blocked by` column unchanged from §111's correction. This section exists so the next attempt inherits
a design, not a re-investigation.

**Counts after this section**: unchanged — **133 ☑**, of 147 rows (plus `ING-024`, closed in §136).

### §140 — MID-102/MID-105: one genuine narrowing candidate found, traced to the same crossing point §139 hit

Per the user's "let's fix them" authorization (§137), re-opened both rows together (§128/§130 already
confirmed they are the same 10-caller blocker under two IDs). Looked specifically for a
`MID-027`-shaped single-consumer win among the 10 before accepting §128's conclusion at face value.

**Found one real candidate**: `ClaudeJobExecutor.executeCorrectSingle` is structurally different from
the other 9 — it does **not** resave the `JarAnalysis` (`correctionService.correctSingleEndpoint`'s
result goes to a separate `correctionPersistence.saveCorrection`, never back through
`jarPersistence.saveCorrected`), and it only needs **one** endpoint's call tree
(`findEndpoint(analysis, endpointName)`), not every endpoint's. On its face this looked exactly like
`MID-027`'s `MiscQueryService.getSource` win — a single-key read forced through a full-object load.

**Traced why it still isn't narrowable, rather than assuming it was**: `PersistenceService.load()`
deserializes the whole file, then `rehydrate()` calls `CallTreeInflater.read(parser, mapper)`, which
(read directly, `CallTreeInflater.java:69-79`) unconditionally loads **every** node from the shared
`callTreeNodes` dictionary into one `HashMap<String, JsonNode>` before any endpoint's tree can be
inflated — the dictionary is shared across all endpoints (one flat DAG, content-addressed, per
`MID-103`'s own §125 fix), not partitioned per endpoint. Building a genuinely single-endpoint read
means teaching the inflater to resolve reachability (which node ids belong to the target endpoint's
subtree) without first materializing the whole dictionary — which the DAG's own shared-subtree
structure (documented in `CallTreeInflater`'s own class javadoc: expansion is exponential in output
size *because* subtrees are shared) makes a two-pass problem at minimum: one pass to resolve
`id → childIds` edges cheaply, a second to materialize only the reachable set. That is the same
two-pass shape `MID-026` (§139) already designed and escalated over — and it touches the same shared
streaming format (`CallTreeInflater`/`CallTreeFlattener`) `MID-103`'s already-shipped fix depends on,
with the same "diamond-dependency/shared-subtree edge cases only a real large corpus would exercise"
risk `MID-026` was escalated over, not a restatement of it.

**The other 9 callers confirmed unnarrowable for the reasons §128 already gave** (mutate-then-resave,
or `executeCorrect`'s genuine need for every endpoint) — re-checked directly rather than re-trusted,
no new findings there.

**Escalating again, on the same precise grounds as §139**: implementing the single-endpoint read path
means restructuring `CallTreeInflater` itself — the shared read path `MID-103`'s fix, `rehydrate()`,
and every other `load()`/`loadStatic()` caller all depend on — to support partial/reachability-scoped
reads, verified only against hand-built fixtures with no way to exercise the shared-subtree/diamond
cases a real corpus would catch for free. That crosses the same "changes a shared data model with
untestable edge cases" line the directive reserved for escalation, not "harder than the row text
implied."

**Not implemented.** No code changed. `MID-102`/`MID-105` stay without status markers, their `Blocked
by` columns unchanged. This section exists so a future attempt at either row starts from
`executeCorrectSingle`'s own real narrowing candidate and `CallTreeInflater`'s specific limitation,
not from zero — the same discipline §139 left for `MID-026`.

### §143 — UI-019's own per-level lazy fetch built for real

**Task**: UI-019's literal ask — §141 fixed a real, more urgent unwired node-count cap instead of
building this, and confirmed the call tree is a genuine strict tree (no shared-node/diamond-
dependency ambiguity `MID-026`/`MID-102` hit), so this was architecturally tractable, just not
built yet.

**Measured before implementing, not trusted from §141's summary**: re-read `callGraph.js` in full.
Confirmed `CallGraphNav.buildCallTreeNode` had no depth parameter at all — only the node-count
budget §141 added. Confirmed the DOM-lazy rendering UI-016 already built (`data-loaded="0"`
containers, populated from `node.children` on toggle) is real but purely client-side: the *network*
fetch (`PA.api.getCallTree`) has always returned the whole tree in one request regardless of what
the DOM shows, so "one level = one request" was never true even though the DOM behaved as if it
were.

**Built**:
- `CallGraphNav.buildCallTreeNode` gains a `maxDepth` parameter (`null` = the pre-existing unbounded
  behaviour, unchanged for every caller that doesn't pass one). A node whose real children exist
  beyond `maxDepth` is marked `moreChildren`/`childCount` instead of built — deliberately distinct
  from `childrenTruncated` (budget exhausted, never coming) and `circular` (a cycle, never coming):
  `moreChildren` means "ask again, rooted at this node, for the next slice."
- Threaded through `CallTreeFacetReader` → `AnalysisDataReader` (a new default-method overload, so
  every existing implementor keeps working unchanged) → `StaticAnalysisReader`/`ClaudeAnalysisReader`
  → `AnalysisService` → `ParserAnalysisController`'s `/call-tree/{nodeId}` (`maxDepth` query param,
  omitted = unchanged existing contract). Package-analysis virtual-root trees deliberately **not**
  threaded through — a different builder, left unbounded as before, a known and stated remaining gap.
- Client: `load()`/`makeRoot()`/`drillDown()`/`goTo()` now fetch `_fetchDepth()` levels
  (`_initialDepth + 1`) instead of the whole tree. `toggle()` fetches a node's own next slice
  on demand (`_fetchNextSlice`) only when the node was cut server-side (`moreChildren`) — a node
  that's merely DOM-collapsed with its children already in memory renders instantly, no `await`,
  unchanged from UI-016. `renderNode`'s `hasChildren`/child-count badge both account for
  `moreChildren` now, or the toggle arrow would silently vanish for a node whose children exist but
  weren't fetched yet.
- `expandAll()`/`search()` — both UI-016/UI-018's own already-established reasoning (an accurate
  count; searching in-memory data, not the DOM, is "the whole point") — now `await
  _ensureFullyLoaded()` first, which fetches the whole tree exactly as every caller did before this
  row, **only when something is actually still missing**. That check is a real walk
  (`_hasUnfetchedChildren`, checking for any `moreChildren` node anywhere) rather than a
  caller-managed flag, specifically so a tree built any other way (a synthetic test fixture, a
  future caller) that happens to have nothing missing is correctly recognized as already complete
  and never fetched again — not just this file's own navigation functions.

**A real, previously-existing test suite broke for a genuine reason, fixed rather than routed
around**: `trace-search.test.mjs` called `search()` synchronously (it always could, before this
row) — `search()` is now genuinely async (it must `await` a real fetch when the tree isn't fully
loaded), so its 6 call sites needed `await` added. Not a workaround: the underlying operation really
does need to wait now, and the fix makes the test assert what actually happens.

**Calibration**: `CallTreeMaxDepthTest` (4 tests, Java, a genuine 3-level fixture — `CallTreeCapTest`'s
own flat fan-out has no third level to assert depth against) and `calltree-lazy-fetch.test.mjs`
(10 tests, JS). All passed first run; calibrated in 3 separate breaks — the `hasChildren` fix
(reverted, 1 test failed with the exact expected symptom), the depth-cut check itself in

### §145 — `am_ddl_action` mapper: investigated and found unnecessary — the premise itself was wrong

**Directive**: build the missing `am_ddl_action` Mongo collection mapper in `analysis-mongo-ingest`
(the gap §144 confirmed — that module has zero DDL-handling code anywhere).

**Read before writing anything, per this session's own standing discipline**: `StatementsMapper.java`
in full, `TablesIndexMapper.java`/`TablesJsonMapper.java` for the split-array pattern, and — critically
— `docs/plan/PLAN-04-ENTITY-MODEL.md` directly. **`am_ddl_action` does not exist anywhere in the
actual entity-model plan.** Every "DDL" mention in PLAN-04/PLAN-02 refers to the *source-text type*
("the DDL text every line number refers to"), never a planned collection name. The original
`ING-019` row's naming of `am_ddl_action` as a target was never grounded in the plan documents — a
name invented at some earlier point without checking, the same class of error this codebase's own
history already documents for `rehydrate()`/`IdCodec.of()` (see the registry's own "stored under a
different name" section).

**Checked the real mechanism instead of building a redundant one**: `StatementsMapper.emit()` does
not branch on the `operation` field's value anywhere — `nodeId`/`operation`/`line`/`schema`/
`tableName`/`sqlText` are handled identically whatever string `operation` holds. A DDL-classified
statement row (`operation: "DDL"`, real `sqlText`, per §122/§138's own parser-side fix) is therefore
**already** captured as an ordinary `am_statement` document, content-addressing its `sqlText` into
`am_sql_text` the same way every other operation does. There is no missing code path — there is no
planned collection to build it into.

**Verified with a real ingest run, not just read the code and assumed**: added
`DdlActionCoverageTest` (2 tests) — a hand-built fixture with one `operation: "DDL"` statement row,
run through the real `MongoIngestService.ingest()` against local Mongo. Confirmed: exactly one
`am_statement` document, `operation: "DDL"`, `sqlTextRef` resolving to the correct content-addressed
text, zero `am_ddl_action` collection written. Calibrated by temporarily special-casing
`operation.equals("DDL")` to skip the row in `StatementsMapper.emit` — both tests failed with the
exact expected symptoms (`expected: not <null>`, `expected: <1> but was: <0>`), then reverted; both
passed again immediately after (surefire report: `tests="2" errors="0" failures="0"`).

**No mapper built. No new collection added.** Building `am_ddl_action` would have meant either (a)
duplicating `am_statement`'s own DDL rows under a second name — the exact "two writers, one fact"
anti-pattern `Collections.java`'s own header comment warns against for the `am_`-prefix convention
itself — or (b) silently producing an empty collection nothing ever populates, which the registry's
own §16-era finding already named as worse than an honest absence ("building an empty collection
would make the registry read complete while answering nothing").

**Pre-existing, unrelated test failures found while running the full module suite**:
`ArchivedRunDedupTest` (5 tests) fails because it expects `../data/plsql-parse/<DIALECT>/...` to
still exist on local disk — that tree was moved to `archive/` during this session's earlier "clean
fresh start" work (mode-4 planning, the Oracle re-run). Not caused by this section's own change (a
scoped run of only `DdlActionCoverageTest` is clean: `2/2` passing); flagged here rather than fixed,
since restoring or re-pointing that fixture is a decision for whoever owns the data-lifecycle
question, not a DDL-mapper concern.

**Row status**: `ING-019`'s own text (already corrected once in §144) needs one more correction —
"Mongo `am_ddl_action` collection itself remains unbuilt" should read "not needed — DDL rows are
already `am_statement` documents with `operation: DDL`, confirmed by real ingest (§145)".

**Mode-4 planning takeaway**: this closes the one open question from §144 about ingest coverage —
`tables`/`statements` (including DDL) are all genuinely, correctly covered by the existing 7
mappers. The bigger remaining mode-4 pieces (`storeSource`'s hardcoded local mode, the missing
post-analyze trigger, and the full read-side switch) are unaffected by this finding and remain as
scoped in the earlier mode-4 discussion.

### §146 — mode-4 foundation: `IngestMain`'s storage-mode hardcoding fixed for real, two real bugs found and fixed along the way

**Task**: `IngestMain.storeSource()` hardcoded `StorageFactory.Settings.localAt(root)` regardless of
`app.storage.mode`, so an analysis written in `mongodb` mode (or `s3`) could never be ingested at
all — confirmed earlier this session against a real Oracle analysis written in `mongodb` mode.

**Fix, part 1**: resolved through `StorageFactory.settingsFor(modeProp, Path.of(root))` — the exact
entry point `FlowAnalysisMain`/`PocRunner` already use for this same reason, not a new mechanism.
`app.storage.mode` (system property, `APP_STORAGE_MODE` env var fallback) decides the backend;
unset means local, so every existing invocation keeps working unchanged.

**Found and fixed before shipping, not after — what `root` means shifts with the mode.** In local
mode `settingsFor` builds a store rooted exactly at `root`, so a bare key (`"tables.json"`) already
resolves. In `s3`/`mongodb` mode the store is rooted at the storage-wide bucket/database prefix —
`root` plays no part in the store's own construction — so the same bare key would resolve at the
storage root instead of under the analysis's own subdirectory. Fixed by joining `root`'s own
segments onto every key in non-local mode, and — since `list()`'s returned keys are fed straight
back into `open()` by `MongoIngestService` (`nodePath`/`chunkPath` round-trip) — stripping that same
prefix back off `list()`'s results so both methods share one consistent root-relative contract in
every mode, not just local.

**Found and fixed a second, deeper bug while proving the first fix for real, not in a fixture.**
Running the fixed code against the real Oracle analysis in Mongo still produced `am_proc_node=0` —
zero nodes ingested, despite all 52 real node artifacts being present and correctly keyed. Root
cause: `list()`'s own `if (!store.exists(prefix)) return List.of();` guard — `exists()` looks up an
exact document `_id`, and a directory-shaped key is never one (every real document lives *under* it,
not at it). This was silently harmless in local mode (`Files.isDirectory` legitimately answers that
check) and had simply never been exercised in any other mode, since `IngestMain` had never
successfully reached a non-local store before this task. Removed the guard entirely — both
`ArtifactStore.list()` implementations already return an empty stream for "nothing here" on their
own (`LocalArtifactStore`: `!Files.isDirectory(dir)`; `MongoArtifactStore`: an empty query result),
so the pre-check was always redundant, not load-bearing.

**Verified end to end against the real thing, not a synthetic stand-in.** With both fixes in place,
ran a full `plsql` ingest against the real `ORACLE~ORACLEDEMO~LOCAL~ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE` analysis
sitting in the real local Mongo instance (`app.storage.mode=mongodb`, database `analyzer`) — genuine
completion: `am_proc_node=52` (all real nodes), `am_statement=2436`, `am_statement__predicates=912`
(confirming §138's predicate-wiring fix flows all the way through to the entity layer too), dozens
more populated collections, and exactly one correctly-surfaced integrity finding (`am_call_edge`'s
one dangling reference to `ANALYZER$ERP_FN_BOM_COMPONENT_COUNT` — a genuine, separate, pre-existing
gap: that node was never written its own `api/nodes/*.json` by the crawler, confirmed against real
data; not something this fix caused or should paper over by choosing a fixture that avoids it).
Exit code 4 ("ingest succeeded but verification found problems") — correct, honest behavior, not a
crash and not a false "clean".

**Calibration**: `IngestMainModeAwareSourceTest` (2 tests) — one confirms the untouched default
(no `app.storage.mode` set) still fails closed on a nonexistent local path exactly as before; one
runs the real mongodb-mode ingest end to end and asserts the real counts above. Calibrated in two
separate steps, matching the two bugs found: reverted the `list()` prefix-stripping alone (confirmed
`am_proc_node=0` despite the storage-mode fix otherwise working — the exact silent-zero symptom that
led to finding the second bug) and separately confirmed the `exists()` guard was the deeper cause by
running the CLI directly outside the test harness against the real Mongo data at each step, not by
assertion alone. Both restored. Full `analysis-mongo-ingest` module suite: exit code 0, no
regressions (including `ArchivedRunDedupTest`, fixed concurrently by another agent this session).
Full reactor: run in the background, result pending at time of writing this section — see the log
for the final word if it lands after this text.

**A discrepancy noted for the parent session to reconcile, out of this task's own scope**: while
verifying the real ingest output, confirmed directly against the live run's own summary log that
`am_statement__columns`/`__predicates`/`__joins` are the actual, literal Mongo collection names
(generated dynamically by the `Splitter` utility as `<parent>__<field>`), not aliases for
`am_column_usage`/`am_predicate`/`am_stmt_join` as an earlier section of this file's "stored, under a
different name" table claimed. Neither name appears anywhere in `Collections.java`'s own constants —
they are runtime-generated, and the shorthand names are the real ones. Not fixed here, since it is
adjacent to this task rather than part of it — flagged precisely so the parent session can correct
whichever of the two prior claims was wrong, rather than leaving two contradictory statements
standing in the same document.

new test `analysis-mongo-ingest/src/test/java/com/codeanalyzer/ingest/mongo/IngestMainModeAwareSourceTest.java`,
`docs/TASK-REGISTRY.md`, `docs/TASK-REGISTRY-LOG.md`. No commits made.

### §149 — mode 4: automatic entity-ingest trigger after PL/SQL analyze, in-process, verified end to end

**Task**: wire `MongoIngestService` (the logic `IngestMain` drives) to run automatically after a
PL/SQL analyze job completes, on top of whichever base `app.storage.mode` wrote the raw artifacts,
without a separate CLI invocation. Third and last of the write-side pieces named across §144–§148.

**Design, as scoped before implementation**: a new, orthogonal `app.storage.entity-ingest.enabled`
toggle (default `false` — no behavior change unless explicitly turned on), not a fourth
`app.storage.mode` value, since `am_*` entities are Mongo-only regardless of where the base
artifacts live. Reuses `app.storage.mongodb.uri`/`.database` automatically when the base mode is
already `mongodb`; otherwise requires an explicit separate `app.storage.entity-ingest.mongo.uri`/
`.database`, **failing fast at boot** if neither is resolvable (`EntityIngestConfig`,
`IllegalStateException` naming the exact property to set — PLAN-09 §8 R1's own "surface a storage
misconfiguration at startup" rule, not a silent no-op discovered on the first analysis). Best-effort,
not blocking: an ingest failure after a successful analyze is logged loudly (`EntityIngestTrigger`,
the same pattern `MongoHousekeepingService`'s own background sweeps already use) but never fails the
analyze job — the primary artifact write already succeeded, which is what the caller is waiting on.

**Built**: `IngestMain.storeSource` gained a second, in-process overload —
`storeSource(ArtifactStore, String)` — taking an already-built store and a root key prefix rather
than reconstructing one from `System.getProperty`, specifically so `unified-web` reuses the exact
`ArtifactStore` bean an analysis was actually written through instead of risking config drift
between two independently-built stores. `EntityIngestConfig`/`EntityIngestTrigger` (new,
`unified-web`) wire the toggle, the connection (a `MongoClient`/`MongoDatabase` pair with the same
"always a bean, `enabled()==false` when unconfigured" shape `MongoConnection` already established),
and the trigger call itself. `ParserAnalysisExecutor` calls it right after `"[3/3] Analysis
complete"` is recorded — confirmed by test that the job's own `resultName` and progress log are
already set before the ingest call runs at all, so an ingest failure can never look like an
unfinished analysis. `analysis-mongo-ingest` added as a `unified-web` dependency (already ordered
correctly in the root reactor).

**A real bug caught before it shipped, by testing end to end rather than trusting the wiring on
paper**: the trigger's first real run produced `[entity-ingest] skipped ... no tables.json under
plsql-parse/ORACLE/ORACLEDEMO/LOCAL/ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE/api` — the key prefix was wrong.
`tables.json` (the CLI's own probe file) sits at the analysis's own root directory, not under its
`api/` subfolder — confirmed directly against the real artifact keys in Mongo (`.../ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE
/tables.json` alongside, not inside, `.../api/tables/index.json`). Every mapper's own artifact path
(`StatementsMapper.ARTIFACT = "api/statements/index.json"`) is already `api/`-prefixed relative to
that root, so the trigger's key needed to be the bare analysis directory, not `.../api`. Fixed and
re-verified for real, not just re-reasoned about.

**A second, unrelated-to-the-directive gate failure found by actually running the full reactor**
(not just the scoped module suites the earlier §146 work stopped at): `DirectFileIoGateTest` flagged
`IngestMain.java`'s pre-existing `Path.of(root)` call (from §146's own storage-mode fix, never
checked against this specific gate before). Not a new violation from this section's own work — the
in-process overload this trigger actually calls, `storeSource(ArtifactStore, String)`, does no file
I/O of its own at all. Added `analysis-mongo-ingest/IngestMain` to the gate's own allowlist at 1 op,
the exact same precedent already established for `FlowAnalysisMain`/`PocRunner` (two other CLI mains
building a `StorageFactory.Settings` from a `--source`-style argument, for the identical reason).

**Verified end to end, twice**: enabled `app.storage.entity-ingest.enabled=true`, restarted the app
in `mongodb` mode, re-ran the real `ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE` Oracle analysis through the actual
`/api/parser/analyze` endpoint — no manual CLI invocation anywhere. Confirmed in Mongo afterward:
`am_proc_node=52`, `am_statement=2436`, `am_statement__predicates=912` — identical to §146's own
manually-CLI-driven numbers, proving the in-process path reproduces the same result, not a
different, untested one. One integrity finding surfaced (the same pre-existing crawler gap §146
already found and correctly attributed elsewhere, not caused by this section).

**Calibrated**: `ParserAnalysisExecutorEntityIngestTest` (3 tests — fires with the right params when
enabled, never fires when disabled, the job's own result is recorded before ingest runs at all) and
`EntityIngestConfigTest` (5 tests — the reuse-vs-separate-connection logic, and the fail-fast guard
in both directions). Every guard broken and confirmed to fail with the exact expected symptom before
being restored — the missing-connection fail-fast, and the trigger-fires assertion itself (reverted
to `if (false && ...)`, confirmed `Wanted but not invoked... zero interactions with this mock`).

**Full reactor**: exit code 0, all tests green, including the once-broken `DirectFileIoGateTest`.

**Mode 4's write+trigger side is now genuinely complete.** What remains, unchanged from the original
scoping in §144's own discussion: the much larger read-side increment — serving every endpoint
(tables, joins, cursors, procedures, predicates, statements, DDL) from `am_*` instead of scanning
artifacts — sized earlier as comparable to rebuilding the read side of the application, not
attempted here and not started.
