### §150 — mode 4 read-side: first facet pilot (`tables`), real equivalence proven, real complexity found

**Directive**: prove the read-side pattern for one facet (`tables`) before repeating it across the
rest of the API surface — deliberately not attempting joins/cursors/sequences/procedures/predicates/
statements/DDL in this section.

**Found before writing any code**: there is no single `am_table` catalogue collection. The entity
model is normalised around `am_node_table_access` (one row per node-table pair — which usefully maps
1:1 onto one `usedBy[]` entry), with operations split into six per-verb child collections
(`am_node_table_access__select/insert/update/delete/merge/dynamic`, `Splitter`'s own naming rule),
and predicates reachable only through `am_statement` → `am_statement__predicates`, keyed by the
statement's own identity, not the table's. Reproducing `ParserFacetSpecs.TABLES`'s row shape from
entities is therefore a **four-collection join in application code**, not a single collection read —
a materially different (and more complex) shape than "swap one artifact read for one Mongo read."

**Built**: `EntityTablesReader` (new), rebuilding the exact `{tables:[{name, schema, objectType,
allOperations, usedBy:[{nodeId, nodeName, operations, predicates}]}]}` shape `ParserFacetSpecs.TABLES`
already expects, so the existing paging/sort/scope machinery (`FacetPageResponder`,
`PlsqlScopeFilter.directTables`/`subtreeTables`) runs completely unchanged on top of it. Wired behind
an explicit, reversible opt-in — `GET /tables/page?source=entity` — via a new `facet(...)` overload
taking a `documentOverride`; every existing call site (`documentOverride=null`) is byte-for-byte
today's behaviour.

**A real bug found only by testing against real data, not a hand-built fixture**: `am_statement`'s
own business-key field is called `entityKey`, not `key` — unlike `am_node_table_access`/`am_run`/
`am_statement__predicates`, which do use `key`. The first version (reading `key`, always null on
`am_statement`) silently produced **zero** predicates rather than an error — confirmed by an
executable test failing at `expected: <912> but was: <0>` before being traced to the field-name
mismatch and fixed. A second real gap found by running the full suite, not just the new test: this
class's six raw Mongo queries tripped `QueryTimeoutGateTest` (every query in this codebase must be
wrapped `QueryBudget.request(...)`, a convention this pilot hadn't yet been checked against) —
fixed by wrapping all six.

**Verified for real, twice**: once via direct HTTP comparison (`/tables/page` vs.
`/tables/page?source=entity` for `ORACLE~ORACLEDEMO~LOCAL~ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE`, both after rebuilding
and restarting the app with the actual new code — an earlier comparison against the *old, unrebuilt*
running jar silently compared the artifact-scan path against itself and was discarded as
non-evidence, not reported as a result), and once via `EntityTablesReaderComparisonTest` (2 tests,
real Mongo, real analysis, skips rather than fails if unavailable). Both agree exactly: **42/42
tables, 912/912 predicates, identical table names, identical per-table operation line counts.**

**Test results**: `EntityTablesReaderComparisonTest` (2), `QueryTimeoutGateTest` (confirmed passing
after the fix), full reactor test suite: **exit code 0, zero errors**.

**Honest assessment for the remaining facets, since that's what determines whether this is worth
continuing**: the pattern (build the exact artifact-scan row shape, opt-in override, leave existing
paging/scope untouched) generalises cleanly and is the right approach to keep using. The *cost per
facet* does not generalise uniformly, though — `tables` needed a 4-collection join; `joins`/`cursors`
(per earlier `ParserFacetSpecs` reading this session) may map more directly onto `am_node_table_access
__joins`/existing cursor-specific entities, while `statements`/`predicates` may be simpler (closer to
a direct `am_statement`/`am_statement__predicates` read) — this needs measuring per facet, not
assumed uniform, the same discipline this pilot itself required. **Not attempted here**: any facet
beyond `tables`, and no `RepositoryMode`-level integration (this pilot deliberately stayed
controller-scoped to limit blast radius while only one facet has entity coverage).

`unified-web/src/test/java/com/plsqlanalyzer/web/parser/controller/ParserAnalysisControllerPlsqlScopeTest.java`
(2 call sites updated for the new `getTablesPage` param), new
`unified-web/src/test/java/com/plsqlanalyzer/web/parser/service/EntityTablesReaderComparisonTest.java`,

### §151 — mode 4 read-side: second facet (`joins`), cheaper join than tables' own, two real ordering bugs caught by testing for real

Second facet in the mode-4 read-side conversion (see §150 for the pilot pattern this replicates):
`GET /analyses/{name}/joins?source=entity`, the same explicit, reversible opt-in as `/tables/page`'s
own `source=entity`.

**Measured before designing anything**: two collections carry join data —
`am_statement__joins` (981 rows, keyed by statement identity) and `am_node_table_access__joins`
(981 rows, keyed by node-table-access identity, the same parent `EntityTablesReader` already reads).
Confirmed by matching row counts these are genuine duplicate views of the same underlying data, not
two sources this facet needs — used `am_node_table_access__joins` alone, since its own
`leftTable`/`joinedTable` fields map directly onto the facet's own row identity. Net: a
two-collection join (`am_node_table_access__joins` → `am_node_table_access` → `am_proc_node`),
cheaper than the tables pilot's four — the honest per-facet cost variance §150 predicted, confirmed
on the very next facet.

**Two real bugs, both caught only by testing against real data, not assumed from the schema alone**:

1. A join sub-document omits `leftTable` entirely when the left side of the join is the row's own
   owning table — an implicit self-reference the crawler doesn't bother repeating. The first version
   dropped these rows outright (`leftTable == null` looked like "no data"), silently losing 2 real
   table pairs and 64 real join usages (a raw Mongo aggregate found 33 pairs; the reader produced
   31). Fixed by falling back to `am_node_table_access`'s own table name when `leftTable` is absent.
2. Even with (1) fixed, a direct HTTP comparison against the real artifact-scan path
   (`/joins` vs. `/joins?source=entity`, both against `ORACLE~ORACLEDEMO~LOCAL~ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE`)
   found row counts still didn't match (33 vs. the artifact's 27), despite identical total access
   details (981 either way). The same logical table pair is recorded with left/right flipped across
   different SQL statements that join the same two tables in opposite directions, and the
   artifact-scan path already merges both directions into one row — this reader was keeping them
   direction-sensitive. Fixed by grouping on the *unordered* pair (sorted), with `leftTable`/
   `rightTable` on the assembled row kept as whichever direction was recorded first — the second bug
   this facet's own scan of the artifact-scan output would not have caught without the real
   comparison, exactly the discipline §150 established.

**Verified twice for real, exactly like §150**: rebuilt and restarted the actual app (not compared
against a stale jar — §150's own flagged failure mode), then compared `/joins` vs.
`/joins?source=entity` directly: **27/27 rows, 981/981 access details, zero per-pair count
mismatches, unordered pair sets identical.** Plus a standalone JUnit test
(`EntityJoinsReaderComparisonTest`, 2 tests) against the same real Mongo data, calibrated by
reverting each of the two fixes independently and confirming the exact expected wrong counts (31
instead of 27, then 33 instead of 27) before restoring both.

**Test results**: 2 new tests, both calibrated. Full reactor (`mvn test`, no `-pl` scoping):
exit code 0, no failures anywhere in the log.

**Cost comparison against `tables` (§150), as promised**: cheaper — a 2-collection join instead of
4, no predicate-shaped complexity, but a genuinely different kind of gotcha (join-direction
canonicalisation) that the tables pilot never had to deal with at all. Confirms §150's own honest
assessment: per-facet cost and per-facet *shape* of difficulty both vary; neither is safely
predictable from the facet's name or from the previous facet's own experience.

Files changed: new `EntityJoinsReader.java`, `ParserAnalysisController.java`, new
`EntityJoinsReaderComparisonTest.java`, `ParserAnalysisControllerPlsqlScopeTest.java` (2 call sites,
compile fix for the new `source` parameter), `docs/TASK-REGISTRY.md`, `docs/TASK-REGISTRY-LOG.md`.
No commits made.

**Remaining mode-4 read-side facets, unchanged in count**: `cursors`, `sequences`, `procedures`,
`predicates`, `statements`, DDL — 5 of ~7 facets not yet attempted.

### §152 — mode 4 read-side: `cursors` facet, cheapest of three so far, one honest unverified limitation

Third facet in the mode-4 read-side series (after `tables` §150, `joins` §151), same pattern:
match the artifact-scan facet's exact row shape, opt-in via `?source=entity`, verified twice for real.

**Built**: `EntityCursorsReader.java`, wired behind `GET /cursors?source=entity`. **Real coverage
measured**: cursor data lives in a single collection, `am_cursor_decl` — one document per cursor
declaration, no split-array children in this corpus (its `stmtOperations` field is empty everywhere,
so `Splitter` never created a child collection for it). One batched join needed: `nodeRef` →
`am_proc_node` for the owning procedure's name/source file — the cheapest of the three facets by
collection-join count (1, vs. `tables`' 4 and `joins`' 2).

**No new bug found this time** — unlike `tables` (business-key field mismatch, gate violation) and
`joins` (dropped-table edge case, direction canonicalization), both comparison tests passed on first
write. **Verified twice for real**: rebuilt/restarted app, direct HTTP comparison — **64/64 rows,
476/476 access details**, identical name/type/detailCount across every row, matched on the first
attempt.

**One honest limitation stated, not hidden**: the reader also reproduces the artifact-scan path's
`stmtOperations` (OPEN/FETCH/CLOSE) branch defensively, mirroring that logic exactly — but this
corpus's own cursors never exercise it, so that branch is **unverified against real data**, stated
plainly in the class's own doc comment rather than implied proven by the clean comparison result.

**Calibrated**: broke the merge key (dropped `::nodeId`), confirmed the exact expected wrong count
(33 instead of 64), restored, reconfirmed clean. Full reactor: exit 0.

**Cost comparison**: `tables` (4-collection join, 2 real bugs) > `joins` (2-collection join, 2 real
bugs) > `cursors` (1-collection join, 0 bugs this time) — confirms per-facet cost and risk both vary
genuinely, not a pattern that gets easier or harder monotonically; each facet still needs its own
real measurement, not an assumption carried from the last one.

**Mode-4 read-side progress: 3 of 8 facets done** (`tables`, `joins`, `cursors`). Remaining:
`sequences`, `procedures`, `predicates`, `statements`, `dynamic-sql`, plus the final mode-wide toggle.

### §153 — mode 4 read-side: `sequences` facet, one collection, one real limitation stated (not hidden)

Fourth facet in the mode-4 read-side series (`tables` §150, `joins` §151, `cursors` §152), same
pattern: match the artifact-scan facet's exact row shape, opt-in via `?source=entity`, verified
twice for real.

**Built**: `EntitySequencesReader.java`, wired behind `GET /sequences?source=entity`. **Real
coverage measured**: `am_sequence_use` — one row per (node, sequence, operation, line), written
directly by `NodeDetailMapper.emitSequences` (never through `Splitter`, since it's built row-by-row
in Java rather than derived from a JSON array of objects) — already carries `sequenceName`/
`schemaName` denormalised onto each use row, so no second join to `am_sequence_obj` was needed
(same reasoning `EntityCursorsReader`'s own denormalised display fields avoided a second lookup).
One batched join needed: `am_sequence_use.nodeRef` → `am_proc_node` for the owning procedure's
display name/id — cheapest join shape yet, tied with `cursors`' own single-collection lookup.

**Verified twice for real**: rebuilt/restarted the app, direct HTTP comparison `/sequences` vs.
`/sequences?source=entity` — **2/2 rows, 34/34 access details**, matched at the field level too
(every operation/procedureId/lineNumber identical per sequence, not just aggregate counts).

**One real limitation stated, not hidden**: the artifact-scan reader (`SequenceFacetReader
.getSequences`) re-derives each use's real line number by scanning the node's own source text for
`SEQ.NEXTVAL`/`NEXT VALUE FOR SEQ`, falling back to the stored line only when that scan finds
nothing (older analyses stored the body-start line for every usage, not the real one).
`am_sequence_use.line` is written straight from the pre-scan value — the entity reader can't
reproduce the source-rescan without its own investigation into where source text lives in entity
storage, out of scope for one facet. On this corpus it made no observed difference (confirmed by the
exact field-level match above), but an analysis with older body-start-line data would show a real
difference between the two paths. Documented in the class's own doc comment.

**Calibrated**: broke the `am_sequence_use` query (added an impossible `operation` filter), confirmed
both tests failed with the exact expected wrong values (0 rows, no real procedure/operation seen),
restored, reconfirmed clean. Full reactor (`mvn test`, no scoping): exit code 0, no failures anywhere.

**Cost comparison**: `tables` (4-collection join, 2 bugs) > `joins` (2-collection join, 2 bugs) >
`cursors`/`sequences` (1-collection join each, 0 new bugs, one stated pre-existing limitation each)
— confirms the pattern keeps generalizing, with cost/risk varying genuinely per facet rather than
trending in either direction.

**Mode-4 read-side progress: 4 of 8 facets done** (`tables`, `joins`, `cursors`, `sequences`).
Remaining: `procedures`, `predicates`, `statements`, `dynamic-sql`, plus the final mode-wide toggle.

### §154 — mode 4 read-side: `procedures` facet escalated — a real, confirmed entity-coverage gap, not built lossy

Fifth facet in the mode-4 read-side series (`tables` §150, `joins` §151, `cursors` §152,
`sequences` §153) — **not built**, escalated instead, per the same discipline every prior facet
used when a real gap was found rather than a guessable one.

**Measured before writing any code**: `ParserFacetSpecs.PROCEDURES` reads `nodeId`, `name`, `schema`,
`depth`, `objectType`, `linesOfCode`, and `counts.exceptionHandlers` (the last one backing UI-029's
hidden `cf=9:Y` filter). `am_proc_node` (written by `NodeDetailMapper`, which ingests
`api/nodes/*.json` — the per-node **detail** file) carries every field except `counts`. Confirmed by
direct inspection, not assumption: `nodeId`/`name`/`schema`/`depth`/`objectType`/`linesOfCode`/
`sourceFile` are all present and correct on a real `am_proc_node` document; `counts` is absent
entirely on the same document — checked on `ANALYZER$ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE`, a node known to have
`counts.exceptionHandlers: 86` (confirmed via the live `/procedures?cf=9:Y` endpoint, which found 39
matching procedures).

**Root cause, traced precisely, not guessed**: `counts` lives only in `api/index.json`'s own
embedded per-node summary array — a different, richer artifact than `api/nodes/*.json` — confirmed
by fetching the same node's raw detail file directly via `/node/{file}` (`counts` absent) versus the
`/procedures` endpoint, which reads `api/index.json` via `IndexFacetReader.getProcedures` (`counts`
present, full object, 86 exception handlers and all). `analysis-mongo-ingest` has **no mapper for
`api/index.json` at all** — only `NodeDetailMapper` for `api/nodes/*.json` — so `counts` (the whole
object: `tables`, `callsOut`, `cursors`, `statements`, `exceptionHandlers`, everything) has no path
into any entity collection today.

**Not built lossy, as the directive required**: faking `exceptionHandlers` as always-0 (or omitting
the hidden column) would make UI-029's `cf=9:Y` filter silently return zero rows under
`?source=entity` instead of the real 39 — a wrong answer indistinguishable from a right one, exactly
the failure class this whole codebase's own conventions exist to prevent. Escalating instead of
shipping that.

**What would actually close this**: either (a) a new mapper for `api/index.json`'s own node array
(measuring first whether its fields are a superset, subset, or genuinely different projection of
`api/nodes/*.json`'s — not assumed), or (b) extending `NodeDetailMapper` to also read `counts` if
it's derivable from data `api/nodes/*.json` already carries elsewhere (e.g. computed from the same
split children `NodeDetailMapper` already emits — `exceptionHandlers` specifically might be a count
of `am_proc_node`'s own already-split `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` child rows, which would mean no new
artifact read is needed at all, just a derived field at ingest time — **this specific possibility is
worth checking first**, since `emitChildren` already writes `Collections.EXCEPTION_HANDLER` rows per
node and counting them would reproduce `exceptionHandlers` without touching `api/index.json`).

**Test results**: none — no code changed, since nothing was implemented against a disproven premise
(that entity coverage was complete enough to proceed).

**Mode-4 read-side progress: 4 of 8 facets done** (`tables`, `joins`, `cursors`, `sequences`),
**1 escalated** (`procedures`). Remaining to attempt: `predicates`, `statements`, `dynamic-sql`, plus
the final mode-wide toggle — `procedures` needs the coverage gap above resolved first.

### §157 — mode 4 read-side: "statements" investigated, found not to be an 8th facet, and disqualified for real once it was checked against real data

**Corrected the count before building anything**: `ParserFacetSpecs` has exactly seven entries
(`TABLES`, `PROCEDURES`, `SEQUENCES`, `CURSORS`, `JOINS`, `DYNAMIC_SQL`, `PREDICATES`) — there is no
pageable `statements` facet at all, so the "8 facets" the mode-4 read-side plan was tracking against
was itself off by one. The only `statements` endpoint in this API is `GET .../statements/summary`
(`StatementsSummaryService`), a per-node aggregation, structurally different from the other seven's
paged-grid shape — the real remaining facet is `dynamic-sql` (facet 7 of the real 7), not "statements
and dynamic-sql" as two separate remaining items.

**Investigated whether an entity-backed version of the summary was buildable anyway.** `am_statement`
looked promising — it's the base collection every other facet reader has already joined into, and
912/912-predicate-clean on the very first attempt in §156. Built `EntityStatementsSummaryReader`,
grouping `am_statement` by `(nodeRef, operation)` to reproduce `counts.statements`'s per-type counts.

**Disqualified by testing against real data before wiring it live** — the same discipline that
caught `tables`/`joins`'s bugs before shipping caught a structural mismatch here instead of a fixable
bug: `counts.statements` counts every statement **occurrence** across 27 real statement types
(SELECT, LOOP, IF, ASSIGNMENT, CURSOR_FOR_LOOP, EXECUTE_IMMEDIATE, CASE, SUBQUERY, RAISE, COMMIT,
RETURN, and more), while `am_statement` only ever has rows for statements that **touch a table** —
confirmed by direct HTTP comparison: only 6 of 27 real types appeared at all, and even the 6 shared
disagreed on count for a structural reason (`am_statement` counts once per table touched; a
multi-table SELECT inflates the derived count — SELECT measured 403 real vs. 2082 derived on the
same corpus). Unlike `procedures`' `exceptionHandlers` gap (§154), there is no lucky already-split
child collection to derive the right unit from here — the real fix would need a new
`api/index.json` mapper, real, separate, future scope, not attempted.

**Did not wire this live.** Reverted the controller's `source=entity` branch and the constructor
wiring entirely rather than leave a plausible-looking opt-in that silently serves wrong aggregate
counts — the exact failure class this whole mode-4 effort exists to prevent. `EntityStatementsSummaryReader.java`
kept as an unused, fully-documented record of the investigation (including a correctly-reusable
scope-predicate pattern for whatever reader eventually needs it), not deleted, so a future attempt
at the real `api/index.json` mapper starts from a real lead instead of zero.

**Compiles clean, test-compile clean, full reactor confirmed: exit code 0, no failures.**

**Mode-4 read-side: 6 of the real 7 facets done** (`tables`, `joins`, `cursors`, `sequences`,
`procedures`, `predicates`). Remaining: `dynamic-sql` (the real 7th, not an 8th), plus the final
mode-wide toggle. The `statements/summary` aggregation stays on artifact-scan permanently until a
real `api/index.json` mapper exists — not a pending mode-4 item, a genuinely separate, larger gap.

### §159 — mode 4: the mode-wide toggle, closing out mode 4 as a genuine, selectable read+write mode

**Task**: the last piece named across §144–§158 — a config flag making entity-backed reads the
default across all 7 real facets, rather than 7 separate per-request `?source=entity` opt-ins.

**Built**: `app.storage.entity-read.enabled` (default `false`, matching every other mode-4 toggle's
own convention). `ParserAnalysisController.useEntitySource(source)`, one shared resolution method
all 7 facet endpoints now call instead of each re-checking `"entity".equals(source)` inline:
an explicit `source=entity`/`source=artifact` request param always wins (how the 7 comparison tests
already force one path or the other); absent that, the config flag decides; never `true` when
`entityIngestConnection` itself isn't configured. All 7 call sites (`getTablesPage`, `getJoins`,
`getCursors`, `getSequences`, `getProcedures`, `getPredicates`, `getDynamicSql`) now route through it.

**A real, immediate side effect caught by compiling, not guessed at**: the new constructor parameter
is a primitive `boolean`, which the three reflection-based controller test builders
(`ParserAnalysisControllerPlsqlScopeTest`, `..PredicatesTest`, `..ProceduresExportTest`) couldn't
construct — `mock(boolean.class)` throws, Mockito cannot mock a primitive. Fixed by adding a
primitive-type branch (`false`/`0`) to all three builders' own parameter-filling loop, the same
reflection-construction pattern this session established back when `AnalyzerControllerFullBodyGateTest`
first needed it for an unrelated constructor change.

**Calibrated**: `ParserAnalysisControllerEntityReadDefaultTest` (3 tests, using `tables` as the
representative facet since the resolution logic itself is facet-agnostic) — default on serves entity
with no `source` param, an explicit `source=artifact` overrides the default even when it's on, and
default off keeps artifact-scan as the default. Broke the override branch, confirmed the exact
expected failure (`NeverWantedButInvoked`, the override test caught the reader being called when it
shouldn't have been), restored.

**Verified for real, not just in tests**: rebuilt and restarted the app with both
`--app.storage.entity-ingest.enabled=true` and `--app.storage.entity-read.enabled=true`, called
`/tables/page`, `/joins`, `/predicates` with **no `source` param at all** against the real
`ORACLE~ORACLEDEMO~LOCAL~ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE` analysis — all three returned the exact entity-side
counts already proven correct in §150/§151/§156 (42 tables, 27 joins, 26/912 predicates), and
`?source=artifact` still forced the artifact-scan path on request.

**Full reactor: exit code 0, zero failures.**

**Mode 4 is now genuinely complete, the culmination of §144 through this section.** It stands
alongside `local`/`s3`/`mongodb` as a real, selectable mode: writes auto-populate `am_*` after every
PL/SQL analyze (§149), and reads can be switched to serve from those same collections by default
(this section) rather than per-request opt-in, with every one of the 7 real facets independently
measured and verified against real data rather than assumed to generalize from the first (`tables`
needed a 4-collection join and found 2 bugs; `cursors`/`sequences`/`predicates` needed 1 collection
each and found none; `procedures` needed a genuine escalation, resolved via a derived count once a
real lead was verified; `statements` was investigated and correctly disqualified rather than shipped
wrong; `dynamic-sql` matched cleanly on the first attempt). No row in the original 147-row registry
tracked mode 4 as a discrete item — it was undertaken as its own initiative at the user's own
direction, and closes here on that same basis.

### §160 — UI-024: `leftPanel.js`'s initial render made threshold-aware, a real fix that still does not close the row

§131 named this file's own remaining blocker precisely: `_renderLeftProcedures` called
`PA.nodeIndex.all()` unconditionally on every load, before `PA._LP_SERVER_FILTER_THRESHOLD`
(MID-002, §39) was ever consulted — the filter/search path was already threshold-aware, the initial
paint that runs before any keystroke was not.

**Fixed**: at or above the threshold, `_renderLeftProcedures` no longer touches `PA.nodeIndex` at
all — it renders the shell immediately (header count from `PA.analysisData.totalNodes`, already
known cheaply since MID-002 dropped `nodes[]` from `/index`) and fetches the first page via the same
`PA.api.searchProcedures('', ...)` route the filter path's own empty-query case already used. Below
the threshold, behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged — the array path this file's own header comment
was measured against, verified by this repo's real 52-procedure corpus staying on it.

**A second bug caught while fixing the first**: `PA.filterLeft`'s own threshold branch read
`PA._lp.proc.all.length` — which this fix deliberately leaves at `0` above the threshold, since the
array is no longer populated there at all. Left unfixed, `filterLeft` would have silently routed
back to the (now-empty) array path for every keystroke on a large analysis. Fixed to check
`PA.analysisData.totalNodes` instead, the same source the initial render now uses.

**Calibrated**: `parser-leftpanel-threshold-render.test.mjs` (3 tests), since no real corpus at
threshold scale (1,000+ procedures) exists in this repo — verified by stubbing
`PA.analysisData.totalNodes` on both sides of the threshold rather than needing one. One real test
authoring bug caught and fixed along the way: an incomplete DOM stub (missing `querySelector`/
`insertAdjacentHTML`) caused the below-threshold test to throw inside `_lpRenderBatch`, which
manifested as a same-process crash in an unrelated, later-run test file rather than a clean
same-test failure — fixed the stub, not the production code, once traced to its real cause. Broke
the fix (`if (false && totalKnown >= ...)`), confirmed the exact expected failure, restored. Full JS
suite: **286 passed, 0 failed** (was 283 before this section's 3 new tests).

**Does not close UI-024.** Checked `app.js`'s `PA.loadAnalysis` again before claiming otherwise:
`result.nodes = await PA.api.getProcedures()` still runs unconditionally on every load, populating
`PA.analysisData.nodes` (and therefore `PA.nodeIndex`) regardless of procedure count or which
consumers actually need it. `leftPanel.js` no longer *requires* that residency for its own initial
render, but the residency itself is still created eagerly, upstream of every consumer including this
one — the same root cause §113/§131 already isolated. Real progress (one more consumer genuinely
converted, following the same pattern that closed 19 of ~19 named call sites over §92-99/§112/§113),
not the row's own closure.

**UI-024 stays `◐`.** Its own real remaining blocker is unchanged from §131's own finding: the
load-time fetch in `app.js`, not any individual consumer file.

### §161 — UI-024: lazy `PA.nodeIndex` infrastructure built and one consumer converted; the real remaining blocker is wider than previously measured

**Attempted the full lazy-nodeIndex conversion**, per the "block render until fetched" design
decided earlier this session (§114/§137) and §131's own measured count (19 real call sites, 11
files, most already async-friendly). Re-verified that count directly (`grep -rn "PA.nodeIndex\."
parser/js/*.js`, excluding comments and `nodeIndex.js` itself) rather than trusting it: confirmed
~16-19 direct call sites across 9-11 files, and traced each to its enclosing function.

**Found the real blocker, by measuring rather than assuming it away**: two of the direct consumers —
`PA.getScopedNodes()` (`scope.js`) and `PA._buildNodeIdMap()` (`utils.js`) — are foundational,
high-fan-in synchronous utilities called from dozens of places across the codebase, not leaf
call sites. §131's own 19-site count measured *direct* `PA.nodeIndex` callers, but did not separately
flag that two of those 19 are themselves utilities with a much wider blast radius one layer up.
Converting either to `async` would cascade through every one of their own callers — a materially
bigger scope than the "19 sites" framing implied, discovered only by tracing the actual call graph,
not by re-reading the old count.

**Scoped down to what was genuinely safe to build and verify**: added `PA.nodeIndex.ensureLoaded()`
— resolves immediately if `PA.analysisData.nodes` is already resident (the common case today, since
`PA.loadAnalysis`'s own eager fetch was deliberately left in place, not removed), otherwise fetches
once and dedupes concurrent callers against the same in-flight promise, keyed to the current
`PA.analysisData` object's identity so a new analysis load never resolves against a stale promise.
Converted `PA._findNodeInData` (3 real call sites, all confirmed already inside async functions
before touching anything) to await it — a real, working demonstration of the lazy pattern, not a
stub.

**Did not remove `PA.loadAnalysis`/`PA.pullData`'s own eager fetch.** Doing so before converting
`getScopedNodes`/`_buildNodeIdMap` (and everything that calls them) would create a real, silent-wrong-
answer window — not a crash, a plausible-looking empty or incomplete result — for every one of their
many callers during the gap between analysis load and the background fetch resolving. That is exactly
the failure class this whole session's own discipline exists to catch, so it was not shipped.

**Calibrated**: 6 new tests (`node-index.test.mjs` — `ensureLoaded`'s cache-hit/cache-miss/dedup/
identity-keying behavior, and `_findNodeInData`'s new lazy path). Verifiable without any corpus at
scale — a miss-then-fetch-then-resolve sequence behaves identically whether the fetched array has 1
node or 100,000; only the *memory win* claim is scale-dependent, and that half remains honestly
unverified, not silently implied proven. Fixed one pre-existing test (`parser-find-node-in-data
.test.mjs`) whose own `PA.nodeIndex` stub predated `ensureLoaded()` and crashed the whole test runner
process outright (not a graceful failure) once `_findNodeInData` became `async` — updated the stub
and every call site to `await`. Calibrated by reverting the `ensureLoaded()` call and confirming the
exact expected failures (2 tests, for the right reason), restored. Full JS suite: **292 passed, 0
failed** (was 286 before this section).

**Row status: UI-024 stays `◐`.** Real, calibrated infrastructure now exists and one consumer
genuinely uses it, but the row's own literal DoD ("no full array in memory") is not met — the eager
fetch remains, deliberately, because removing it safely needs `getScopedNodes`/`_buildNodeIdMap`
converted first, and that is real, separate, larger-than-previously-measured scope: not "19 sites,"
but those 19 sites plus however many additional callers those two utilities themselves have. Left as
the row's own next, more precisely-scoped increment rather than closed on partial progress.

### §162 — UI-024: `getScopedNodes`/`_buildNodeIdMap` converted for real — §161's "dozens of callers" fear did not survive tracing the actual call graph

**Re-traced the real call graph before converting anything, per the directive.** §161 declined to
convert `PA.getScopedNodes` (`scope.js`) and `PA._buildNodeIdMap` (`utils.js`) on the assumption
they were "foundational, high-fan-in" utilities with a much wider blast radius than the row's own
19-site count. Traced every real caller directly (`grep -rn`, not re-reading the prior estimate) and
found the fear did not hold once measured:

- `PA.getScopedNodes` has **exactly one real caller** — `export.js`'s own `_gather`, already
  `async`. The `api.js`/`summary.js` hits §161 may have been alluding to are doc comments, not
  calls — matching §99's own earlier, independent finding about this exact function.
- `PA._buildNodeIdMap`'s only real callers are `app.js`'s `PA.showProcedure`/`PA.loadNodeDetail`
  (both already `async`) and `PA._collectTreeNodeIds` — a recursive function that only ever needed
  `idMap` computed **once**, at the top of the recursion, then threaded through unchanged. No
  cascade beyond these four real call sites existed to find.

**Converted**: `getScopedNodes` and `_buildNodeIdMap` now `await PA.nodeIndex.ensureLoaded()`

### §166 — MID-026: the diamond-dependency worry resolved as a non-issue; a real, different, previously-unfound blocker discovered instead

Re-opened per this task's own directive: re-examine whether §111/§139's "no way to verify
diamond-dependency/shared-subtree/cross-package edge cases without a large real corpus" premise
actually holds, the same way several UI-024 "blockers" this session dissolved on direct measurement
rather than requiring the large fixture originally assumed.

**The diamond/shared-subtree worry does not hold up, checked directly against the code, not assumed
either way.** `computeSubtreeDescendants` (the DFS the two-pass design's own subtree computation
depends on) operates purely on `childrenMap`, itself built purely from `FlowEdge` objects — small,
always-resident, structurally independent of whether `FlowNode` bodies are fully materialized or
reduced to a lightweight summary. A node reachable via two parents, or two parents sharing a
subtree, is exactly the case `subtreeCache`'s own memoization already handles correctly today, and
the two-pass redesign changes *which fields of a `FlowNode` are held in memory*, not the graph
traversal itself. There was no real correctness risk here to be unprovable in the first place —
before writing a single line of the redesign, or even building the synthetic fixture the directive
asked for, reading `computeSubtreeDescendants` end to end settled this.

**A real, different, previously-unfound blocker exists instead, discovered by tracing every real
caller of `mergeChunks` rather than only `ChunkedFlowWriter`'s own internals** (§111/§139 measured
`writeApiFiles`/`buildSubtreeTables` in detail but not `mergeChunks`'s callers outside the class):
`DependencyCrawler.computeNodeMetrics(result.getFlowNodes(), result.getCallGraph())` runs as a
discrete step **between** `chunkedWriter.mergeChunks(...)` and `chunkedWriter.writeFinalResult(...)`,
and it **mutates the full `FlowNode` objects in place** — `linesOfCode` (recomputed from
`lineEnd - lineStart`), `statementSummary`, `callCount`, and `calledBy` are all written directly onto
the same node objects `mergeChunks` returned, and `writeApiFiles`'s own detail-writing loop must see
those mutations (the UI's "Call Count" column and per-node LOC both depend on them).

**Why this blocks the two-pass design as written, precisely**: any redesign that has `mergeChunks`
return only lightweight per-node summaries (discarding full `FlowNode` bodies, per §139's own design)
breaks `computeNodeMetrics` silently — either it has nothing to mutate, or it mutates transient
objects `writeApiFiles`'s later chunk re-read would never see. A correct redesign needs
`computeNodeMetrics`'s own logic (which is itself a full pass over every node and every edge, with
its own `nodeIndex`/`findMatchingNodeId` construction, duplicating machinery `writeApiFiles` already
has) moved into `ChunkedFlowWriter`'s own two-pass structure — computed once, alongside the
lightweight per-node summary in pass one, then merged into each node's detail file in pass two. This
is real, additional design scope §139's own write-up did not account for, not a restatement of its
"unprovable without a big corpus" reasoning — that reasoning is now retired, replaced with a precise,
different, and equally real reason.

**Not implemented.** The corrected scope (three `ChunkedFlowWriter` methods per §139, plus
`DependencyCrawler.computeNodeMetrics`'s own logic folded in) is bigger than what a single pass
committed to safely, verified only by hand-built fixtures with no live corpus to catch a coupling
this specific investigation itself only found by tracing every real caller, not by inspecting
`ChunkedFlowWriter` alone. Escalating with this exact, corrected design recorded, so the next attempt
starts from `computeNodeMetrics`'s real coupling, not from a re-derivation of the (now-resolved)
diamond-dependency question.

**No code changed.** `MID-026` stays open, unmarked. Full reactor not re-run (no code touched).

### §167 — MID-026: `computeNodeMetrics`'s own blocker resolved by classification — 3 of 4 outputs are free, the 4th has a clear home; full rewrite still not attempted

Continuing §166's find: `DependencyCrawler.computeNodeMetrics` runs on `result.getFlowNodes()`
right after `mergeChunks` returns (`DependencyCrawler.java:767`), mutating four fields in place, and
`writeFinalResult` → `writeApiFiles` genuinely consumes three of them in the real artifacts —
confirmed by reading `ChunkedFlowWriter.java` directly at every write site, not assumed:

- **`linesOfCode`** — `idx.put("linesOfCode", ...)` (line 580), `detail.put("linesOfCode", ...)`
  (line 811), and a subtree-total aggregation (lines 656-681) that sums a node's own
  `linesOfCode` plus every descendant's. **Category (a): free.** The computation
  (`lineEnd - lineStart + 1`) needs only two scalars already native to a lightweight per-node
  projection — no full body required, in the first pass or anywhere else.
- **`callCount`** — `idx.put("callCount", ...)` (line 584). **Category (a): free.** Computed
  purely from `edges` (a `List<FlowEdge>`, not `FlowNode` bodies) matched against a nodeId-only
  index — the exact same "edges only, no bodies" shape §166 already proved safe for
  `computeSubtreeDescendants`.
- **`calledBy`** — computed the same edge-only way as `callCount`, but **grepped for every
  write site in `ChunkedFlowWriter.java` and found zero** — it is never written into any real
  `api/*.json` artifact, only ever reachable via the optional `flow.json` dump
  (`-Dplsql.write-flow-json=true`, off by default, "nothing reads it" per this file's own
  existing comment). Same class of already-found dead output as `MID-103`'s own `sidecars` —
  free to compute either way (it's edge-only, category (a) regardless), but not load-bearing.
- **`statementSummary`** — `counts.put("statements", ...)` (line 632), read from
  `n.getStatements()`, the full per-node statement list. **Category (c): genuinely needs the
  heavy body.** Not a blocker on the redesign, though — the second pass (already re-reading
  each chunk's full detail individually per §111/§139's own design) is exactly where this
  belongs: compute it there, per node, at the point its full body is already back in memory for
  the writer that needs it, rather than requiring every node's full body resident simultaneously
  in the lightweight first pass.

**Net finding: `computeNodeMetrics` is not a structural blocker at all.** Three of its four
outputs are free in the lightweight first pass (the same one already computing adjacency/subtree
data); the fourth has an exact, uncontrived home in the second pass the design already has. This
closes out the second concrete concern raised against the two-pass redesign (after §166 closed the
first, diamond-dependency one) without finding anything that actually blocks it.

**Not attempted in this section: the full implementation.** Building the redesigned
`ChunkedFlowWriter`/`DependencyCrawler` split, the synthetic diamond/shared-subtree/cross-package
fixture, and byte-identical verification against both that fixture and the real corpus is a
rewrite on the scale of this class itself (comparable to `MID-103`'s own dedicated implementation
effort) — real, bounded, and now free of every specific concern raised against it across §111,
§139, §166, and this section, but not something to attempt and only partially verify inside this
same pass. Recorded as the row's precise remaining shape: a known-safe design with zero open
technical objections, awaiting the implementation pass itself.

**Row status**: `MID-026` stays open, unmarked — genuinely closer to done than at any prior point
(every specific risk raised against the redesign has now been individually resolved), but the code
itself does not yet exist.

### §168 — MID-026: attempted the implementation; found the "lightweight pass" is far bigger than §111/§139 scoped it, before writing anything unsafe

Attempted the actual implementation per this task's own directive, now that §166/§167 retired both
specific concerns raised against the two-pass design. Read `writeApiFiles` in full — the method the
design's own "lightweight first pass" would need to serve — before building the synthetic fixture or
touching any code, the same discipline that caught the diamond-dependency non-issue and the
`computeNodeMetrics` coupling in the two prior sections.

**Real, corrective finding: the "lightweight `{nodeId, tableOperations, linesOfCode}` projection"
§111/§139 originally scoped is far too narrow.** `writeApiFiles`'s own `index.json` writer — the
very first thing the lightweight pass exists to serve — reads directly from `FlowNode.getCalls()`
(for `callsOut`/`internalCalls`/`externalCalls`/sequence-usage counts), `getLocalVariables()`,
`getCursors()`, `getParameters()`, `getExceptionHandlers()` (four `.size()` counts), and
`getTriggerTable/Event/Timing()`/`getMessage()`/`isReadable()` (scalar metadata) — none of which
were in the originally-scoped 3-field projection. Checked `FlowNode`'s own field list directly:
it carries **9 array-typed fields** (`parameters`, `localVariables`, `statements`, `calls`,
`cursors`, `dynamicSql`, `tableOperations`, `exceptionHandlers`, `externalPackageVarRefs`), and
`writeApiFiles`'s `index.json` section alone genuinely needs **7 of the 9** simultaneously resident
across every node (to compute per-node *and per-descendant* counts via `subtreeCache`) — not the 1
(`tableOperations`) the design assumed.

**Only `statements[]` is confirmed the one genuinely droppable field** — the same one §167 already
found `computeNodeMetrics`'s `statementSummary` needs from the heavy body, and independently
confirmed elsewhere in this codebase's own history as the largest artifact by a wide margin (20.7 MB
/ 15,824 rows across five dialects, measured in an earlier session). `dynamicSql` is read only in the
per-node detail writer (a separate section, already one-node-at-a-time in spirit), not `index.json`'s
own all-nodes-at-once pass — a second, smaller candidate for deferral, not yet confirmed safe to
defer the way `statements[]` is.

**Not a blocker — a corrected scope.** The two-pass split is still real and still valid: pass one
becomes "every `FlowNode` field except `statements[]` (and possibly `dynamicSql[]`)," not the
3-field sketch originally written down; pass two re-reads each chunk's full body only for
`statements[]`-dependent work (`computeNodeMetrics`'s `statementSummary`, and whatever in the node
detail writer needs the full statement list). This is a real, expected memory win (statements is the
dominant per-node cost) but a smaller one than "9 fields down to 3" implied, and a **mechanically
much larger rewrite** than previously scoped — touching 7 of `FlowNode`'s field read sites across
`writeApiFiles` instead of 1, each needing its own lightweight-DTO equivalent built and verified.

**Correctly not attempted half-verified.** Building the actual lightweight-node DTO, rewriting all 7
field-read sites in `writeApiFiles` to use it, constructing the synthetic diamond/shared-subtree
fixture, and proving byte-identical output across every `api/*.json` file this method writes is now
known to be a larger mechanical undertaking than either prior section found — genuinely comparable to
`MID-103`'s own dedicated implementation effort, not something to attempt inside the remaining budget
of this same pass without risking exactly the kind of unverified, silently-wrong change this
session's own discipline exists to prevent. No code changed.

**Row status**: `MID-026` stays open, unmarked. Three concerns now resolved in sequence
(diamond-dependency: not real; `computeNodeMetrics`: classified and homed; lightweight-pass scope:
corrected from 3 fields to 7-of-9) — the design keeps getting more precisely known and more clearly
still real, but the implementation itself remains a dedicated future task, now scoped accurately
enough that whoever attempts it next knows the true size of the DTO they need to build.

### §169 — MID-026: first consumer (`writeTableIndex`) converted for real, proving the pattern; full closure still ahead

Sixth pass on this row. Two intervening investigation-only passes (not previously written up — doing
so here alongside this section's own findings, so the record is complete) found: (1) `writeApiFiles`
genuinely has **3** per-node loops needing full bodies, not the 1-2 earlier sections assumed —
`indexNodes`, a separate flow-wide transaction-aggregation loop reading `statements[]` across every
node in one pass (previously unfound), and the node-detail loop — plus 4 more methods
(`writeTableIndex`, `writeStatementIndex`, `writeCallGraph`, `writeNodeIdMap`) taking the full list
as a parameter; (2) re-tracing every cross-node read directly found the *cross-node* need is actually
narrow — only `{tableOperations, linesOfCode, packageName, objectName, schema, nodeId}` must be
resident for every node simultaneously (subtree/cross-node math); every heavy field
(`calls`/`localVariables`/`cursors`/`parameters`/`exceptionHandlers`/`dynamicSql`/`statements`) is
read only within a per-node loop, for that same node, and can stream one node at a time. Net: 7
distinct consumers, genuinely streamable, nothing structurally blocking — but too large to convert
and verify all at once safely.

**New strategy applied, matching mode-4's own one-facet-at-a-time discipline (§150-158, 8 facets each
independently verified) rather than one all-at-once rewrite**: convert **exactly one** of the 7
consumers this pass, fully proven, leaving the other 6 untouched and the codebase in a completely
working state throughout.

**Picked `writeTableIndex`** — verified directly (not assumed) that it has **zero graph/subtree

### §173 — MID-026: own-node index-counts loop investigated, found to overlap with the detail loop, not converted

Attempted the 5th piece in the bounded-conversion series (§169-172 converted 4 consumer methods to
`LightNode`) — `writeApiFiles`'s own-node index-counts loop (builds `index.json`'s per-node summary:
`tableCount`, `callCountOut`/`internalCallCount`/`externalCallCount`, `varCount`, `cursorCount`,
`paramCount`, `exHandlerCount`, `sequenceCount`, plus scalars like `linesOfCode`/`callCount`).

**Read the loop's actual body before converting anything, rather than trust the prior investigation's
own "lightest of the 3 remaining" framing.** It reads `node.getCalls()`, `node.getLocalVariables()`,
`node.getCursors()`, `node.getParameters()`, `node.getExceptionHandlers()` — full-body list fields,
not the lightweight scalars `LightNode` currently carries. This directly contradicts the assumption
this would be the simplest remaining piece; it needs nearly the same heavy fields as piece 3
(`nodes/{id}.json`'s own detail loop), which was already known to need full bodies.

**Real finding, not a repeat of an old one**: pieces 1 and 3 overlap enough in their per-node field
needs that they may be better converted *together*, as one per-node streaming pass computing both
the index summary and the full detail from the same single chunk re-read — not two separate,
independently-converted loops. This is consistent with, and refines, the "own-node use, not
cross-node use" principle the prior investigation established: the fields are only ever needed one
node at a time, so a genuine per-chunk streaming pass (read this node's chunk, compute both its index
counts and its full detail, discard, move to the next node) would work — but building that streaming
pass correctly, with its own synthetic-fixture proof and byte-identical verification, is a real
implementation task on the scale of the earlier 4 conversions combined, not a bounded single-loop
swap like `writeTableIndex`/`writeStatementIndex`/`writeCallGraph`/`writeNodeIdMap` each was.

**Not attempted this pass.** Forcing a partial conversion of just the count-computation half, while
leaving `nodes/{id}.json`'s detail loop reading the same fields from the full list separately, would
mean building (and needing to verify) the per-node chunk re-read machinery twice in slightly
different shapes — real duplicated risk for no size reduction, since both loops would still need to
hold the same heavy per-node data resident during their own pass regardless.

**Row status**: `MID-026` stays open — still 4 of 7 pieces converted (`writeTableIndex`,
`writeStatementIndex`, `writeCallGraph`, `writeNodeIdMap`). The real remaining scope is now named
more precisely than before: a combined per-node streaming pass covering both the index-counts loop
and the detail loop together, plus the separate flow-wide transaction-aggregation loop (reads
`statements[]` across every node, the heaviest single piece) — 2 real remaining pieces, not 3,
once the overlap is accounted for. No code changed this section.

### §174 — MID-026: the missing per-chunk re-read primitive built and proven, in isolation

The combined index+detail streaming pass (attempted right after §173) found the real reason none of
the remaining pieces fit the prior 4 conversions' shape: every one of those 4 (`writeTableIndex`,
`writeStatementIndex`, `writeCallGraph`, `writeNodeIdMap`) was additive — `LightNode` is projected
off the still-fully-resident `List<FlowNode>` `mergeChunks` already builds, so converting a consumer
was a parameter-type swap, not new I/O. The 2 remaining pieces (the combined index+detail loop, and
the transaction-aggregation loop) genuinely need per-node heavy bodies for their own computations,
and **no mechanism existed anywhere in `ChunkedFlowWriter` to re-read one node's full body from its
chunk file on demand** — real new capability, not reuse.

**Built, in isolation, per this session's own bounded-increment discipline — not wired into either
remaining loop yet.** Confirmed chunk files are named `chunk_%04d.json` by write order
(`writeChunk`), not by node id, so a chunk cannot be located by name alone. `buildChunkIndex()`
reads every chunk exactly once (the same single pass `mergeChunks` itself already does) and keeps
only the resulting `nodeId -> ArtifactKey` map — full bodies read during index construction are
discarded immediately after their id is extracted, the same "read once, project, discard" shape as
`toLightNode`, applied to file location instead of field selection. `readNodeChunk(nodeId, index)`
re-reads one node's full body on demand; returns `null` for a dangling id rather than throwing,
matching `writeStatementIndex`'s own established "record it, don't crash" precedent for a missing
reference.

**Calibrated**: `ChunkIndexReadTest` (3 tests) — proves `readNodeChunk` reproduces exactly what
`mergeChunks`'s own full read produces for the same node, the index covers every written chunk, and
a dangling id returns `null` cleanly. Broke `readNodeChunk` (hardcoded `null` return), confirmed the
exact expected failure (`expected: not <null>`), restored, reconfirmed clean.

**Full reactor: exit code 0.** Nothing else changed — the primitive has no caller yet in production
code, by design, so this section proves the primitive alone works before either of the 2 remaining
loops is converted to use it.

**Row status**: `MID-026` stays open at **4 of 7 pieces converted**, plus this new, proven, ready-to-use
primitive. The 2 remaining pieces (combined index+detail loop, transaction-aggregation loop) can now
be attempted using `buildChunkIndex()`/`readNodeChunk()` — a real, unblocked next step, not another
open design question.

### §175 — MID-026: complete caller audit of `FlowResult.getFlowNodes()`, and a real correction to §167's own earlier finding

**Directive**: audit every real caller of `FlowResult.getFlowNodes()`/`setFlowNodes()` across the
whole codebase (not just `ChunkedFlowWriter`), pure investigation, no code changed — feeding the
next implementation pass on whether `mergeChunks`'s eager `List<FlowNode> allNodes` can finally be
removed.

**Complete caller list** (grepped `getFlowNodes()`, `setFlowNodes(`, and `.flowNodes` field access
across the entire repo — `analyzer-storage`'s own unrelated `flowNodes` field on
`MongoPlsqlEntityIndex`, a private `MongoCollection`, is a different class/concern entirely, not a
real hit):

1. **`ChunkedFlowWriter.java:539`** (`writeApiFiles`'s `List<FlowNode> nodes = result.getFlowNodes();`)
   — already the known, already-scoped target of pieces 5–6 (the combined index+detail streaming
   pass and the transaction-aggregation loop). No new information.
2. **`ChunkedFlowWriter.java:204`** (`mergeChunks`'s own `result.setFlowNodes(allNodes);`) — the
   write side itself; this is the line that would change.
3. **`DependencyCrawler.java:767`** (`computeNodeMetrics(result.getFlowNodes(), result.getCallGraph())`)
   — **a real, previously-mischaracterized blocker.** Read `computeNodeMetrics` itself (not just
   confirmed `getStatementSummary()`'s read-side field type, which is what §167 checked): it directly
   calls `n.getStatements()` — the heavy full statement list — on **every node**, to *build*
   `statementSummary` in the first place (lines 994–1008). §167's finding ("`statementSummary` is
   already a cheap precomputed Map, not the heavy list") was correct about how the field reads
   elsewhere afterward, but did not check what computes it — this is that computation, and it is a
   real per-node full-body need. **Not an unsplittable blocker though**: `computeNodeMetrics` has two
   independent phases — a **per-node** phase (`linesOfCode`, `statementSummary`, lines 994–1008,
   needs only that one node's own body) and a **cross-node** phase (`callCount`/`calledBy` from
   `edges` matched against a `nodeId` index, lines 1010–1037, needs no node bodies at all, already
   `LightNode`-compatible per §166/167). The per-node phase can fold into the same per-chunk
   streaming pass pieces 5–6 already plan to build (read a node's chunk once, compute its index
   counts, its `nodes/{id}.json` detail, AND its own `linesOfCode`/`statementSummary`, discard) — it
   is not a new, separate blocker, it is one more thing that belongs in that same planned pass.
4. **`ChunkedFlowWriter.writeFinalResult` → `flow.json`'s debug dump** (`writeJson(flowJson, result)`,
   passing the whole `result` object) — gated behind `writeFlowJsonEnabled()`, which defaults to
   **false** (`-Dplsql.write-flow-json=true` to opt in, per the class's own existing doc comment).
   Not a blocker for the default path. If explicitly re-enabled by an operator for debugging, this
   would still need a full list — an acceptable, explicitly-stated design tradeoff (debug-only mode
   keeps the eager build; default mode does not), not a reason to block the default path's redesign.
5. **Test call sites** (`ChunkIndexReadTest.java:73`, `ChunkedFlowWriterErrorTest.java:55,75,219`) —
   all assert directly against `result.getFlowNodes()`'s count/emptiness/contents. Real callers, but
   straightforwardly updatable alongside whatever the final contract becomes (e.g. if `mergeChunks`
   stops returning every body by default, these tests move to assert against the chunk index / the
   per-node reader instead) — not blockers, adjustment work bundled into the implementation pass.

**Verdict**: `mergeChunks`'s eager full-list construction is **not yet safely removable as a drop-in
change**, but the remaining scope is now fully and precisely known, not vague: (a) fold
`computeNodeMetrics`'s per-node phase into pieces 5–6's already-planned combined streaming pass, (b)
keep its cross-node phase working off `LightNode`+edges as already established, (c) special-case
`flow.json`'s opt-in debug dump to still build a full list only when that flag is set, (d) update the
4 test call sites to match. No further undiscovered callers exist anywhere in the codebase — this
audit is exhaustive, not partial.

**No code changed.** `MID-026` stays at 4 of 7 pieces converted plus the proven `readNodeChunk()`
primitive (§174). This section exists so the next implementation pass has the complete, correct map
— including retracting §167's own incomplete characterization of `statementSummary` — rather than
re-discovering `computeNodeMetrics`'s real shape from scratch again.

### §176 — MID-026: `nodeIndex` itself converted to `LightNode` across every cross-node lookup in `writeApiFiles`, two more dead parameters removed

**Directive**: a final implementation pass, given §174's proven `readNodeChunk()` primitive and
§175's exhaustive caller audit. Full removal of `mergeChunks`'s eager `List<FlowNode> allNodes` was
judged, again, too large to attempt blind in one pass — same conclusion every prior pass reached —
so this pass scoped down to a smaller, real, additive piece that no prior pass had done: the
`nodeIndex` map itself, built once near the top of `writeApiFiles` and used throughout for every
cross-node lookup (edge resolution, subtree DFS, cycle detection, subtree table aggregation), was
still `Map<String, FlowNode>` even after 4 consumers downstream of it had been converted to
`LightNode`. Read every one of those lookups directly (not assumed): each one only ever reads
`tableOperations`, `packageName`/`objectName`/`schema` (via `getPackageName()`/`getObjectName()`),
and `linesOfCode` — one field `LightNode` didn't carry yet.

**Changes**:
1. `LightNode` gained a `linesOfCode` field (13th field) and `getLinesOfCode()` accessor;
   `toLightNode()` extended to populate it from `n.getLinesOfCode()`.
2. `nodeIndex`'s construction switched from `Map<String, FlowNode>` (looping `nodes` directly) to
   `Map<String, LightNode>` (looping `toLightNodes(nodes)`), reusing the same `lightNodes` list
   already built for the 4 existing converted consumers rather than projecting twice.
3. Every cross-node lookup against `nodeIndex` (3 descendant-LOC/table sites, the cycle-path-naming
   site, `findMatchingNodeId`, `detectCycles`) retyped from `FlowNode` to `LightNode` at the call
   site — bodies unchanged, since none of them read anything beyond what `LightNode` now carries.
4. `buildSubtreeTables`'s own `node` parameter was found to be dead — never read, every node in
   `subtreeNodeIds` (including `nodeId` itself) is re-fetched from `nodeIndex` inside its own loop —
   the identical "unused parameter" shape §171 found in `writeCallGraph`. Removed rather than
   converted, citing that precedent directly in the new doc comment.
5. The redundant second `lightNodes`/`lightNodeIndex` projection that previously existed further
   down `writeApiFiles` (built again, separately, right before the `writeTableIndex`/`writeCallGraph`/
   `writeNodeIdMap`/`writeStatementIndex` calls) was removed — those 4 calls now reuse the single
   `lightNodes`/`nodeIndex` built once near the top of the method.

**This does not, on its own, stop `mergeChunks` from building the full `nodes` list** — the two
per-node loops later in `writeApiFiles` (index-counts, `nodes/{id}.json` detail) still iterate
`nodes` directly for each node's own heavy fields, and folding those into the per-chunk streaming
pass §174's `readNodeChunk()` was built for — along with `computeNodeMetrics`'s per-node phase per
§175 — remains the real, larger, not-yet-attempted final step. What this pass does establish, newly
and for real: **every cross-node lookup in `writeApiFiles`, without exception, now reads the
lightweight projection, never another node's full body** — a fact that was assumed true after §166's
"read once, project, discard" framing but had not actually been made true until this pass, since
`nodeIndex` itself — the shared lookup table every one of those cross-node reads goes through — was
still typed `Map<String, FlowNode>` until now.

### §177 — MID-026: the DependencyCrawler mutation coupling fixed for real, 6th piece done

The real blocker identified after 5 prior passes: `DependencyCrawler.computeNodeMetrics` mutated
`FlowNode` objects in place (`setLinesOfCode`/`setStatementSummary`/`setCallCount`/`setCalledBy`),
and `ChunkedFlowWriter.writeApiFiles`'s remaining 2 loops read those mutated fields later off the
same object instances — shared mutable object identity as the data-passing mechanism, which breaks
if nodes are streamed one-at-a-time and discarded.

**Fixed by tracing each of the 4 fields to what actually reads them, not assuming all 4 matter
equally:**
- `linesOfCode` — already set during node construction, earlier in the crawl (confirmed: 3 other
  `setLinesOfCode` call sites exist in `DependencyCrawler` before chunking). `computeNodeMetrics`'s
  own recomputation was a harmless no-op. Left untouched.

### §179 — MID-026: the dedup-mutation blocker fixed for real; `writeApiFiles` fully streaming; `mergeChunks` itself left eager on purpose, a genuine wall not a shortcut

§178 named the exact remaining blocker precisely: `writeApiFiles`'s short-id dedup step mutates
`FlowNode.setNodeId(...)` in place, and the 2 remaining heavy loops read that post-mutation id off
the same object — incompatible with streaming a fresh `FlowNode` per node from its chunk. This pass
built and verified the named fix.

**Built**: `buildLightNodes()` — a new method reading every chunk once via `listSorted`, projecting
straight to `LightNode`, discarding the body (`buildChunkIndex()`'s own "read once, project, discard"
shape, over the full node instead of just its id). Deliberately a `List`, not a `Map`: `buildChunkIndex()`'s
own map silently keeps only the last write if two chunks ever share a raw `nodeId` — a real, latent
limitation of that already-shipped §174 primitive, confirmed still unexercised on the real 52-node
corpus (checked live: zero `$2`/`$3`-suffixed ids exist), documented in `buildLightNodes()`'s own doc
comment rather than silently repeated or silently fixed out of scope.

The dedup algorithm itself (`shortIdCount`/`shortIdSeq`) now runs over this `List<LightNode>`,
producing `List<ResolvedNode(originalId, LightNode resolved)>` — a `withNodeId(LightNode, String)`
helper builds a new record with the resolved id instead of mutating anything (records are immutable
by construction, so this was never optional). All 3 places in `writeApiFiles` that used to iterate
`result.getFlowNodes()` directly (the index+detail-writing loop, the transaction-aggregation loop,
and the `nodes/{id}.json` detail loop) now iterate `resolvedNodes`, re-read each node's full body via
`readNodeChunk(rn.originalId(), chunkIndex)`, `continue` past a `null` (dangling chunk, same
graceful handling as every other §174-based consumer), then call
`node.setNodeId(rn.light().getNodeId())` on that fresh, throwaway instance before running the
existing body unchanged — safe because this instance is never shared with another loop or held past
its own iteration, unlike the old shared-mutation approach it replaces.

**Verified for real, end to end**: rebuilt, restarted the app (port 8083), ran a fresh Oracle analysis
of `ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE` via `/api/parser/analyze` → `/api/queue/{jobId}` polling to `COMPLETE`, then ran

comparison: it predated §177's `statementSummary` fix entirely — all 52 nodes showed

### §180 — source-file storage plan (PL/SQL `.sql` and JAR decompiled `.java`), investigation + proposal, no implementation

**User's ask**: a concrete plan for how procedure/class source gets stored, using GridFS where it helps, explicitly avoiding "all saved in one" (which would complicate reading/writing individual files), for both the JAR analyzer and the PL/SQL parser data sources.

**PL/SQL side — already correct today, confirmed against real data, no gap**: `ChunkedFlowWriter`'s `sourcesKey` writes one `ArtifactKey` per source object (`sources/<SCHEMA>.<OBJECT_NAME>.<ext>`) — genuinely one document/object/file per procedure, not a bundle. Confirmed directly against the live `analyzer` Mongo database: `data/plsql-parse/ORACLE/ORACLEDEMO/LOCAL/ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE/sources/ANALYZER.ERP_FN_BOM_COMPONENT_COUNT.fnc` is its own `artifacts` document, `353` bytes, stored `inline` (base64 field on the manifest document, not GridFS) — real proc source sizes are far under the 1 MiB inline threshold, so GridFS never even engages for a typical `.sql`/`.fnc` file, and doesn't need to. **The "not all in one" requirement is already met by the existing per-`ArtifactKey` design in every storage mode** (local: one file per object; S3: one object per key; mongodb: one manifest document per key, falling back to GridFS automatically and individually only if a single file happens to exceed the threshold — still never bundled with others).

**Mode 4 (entity-read) and source access**: confirmed `/source/{file}` has no `source=entity` branch at all — it always reads through the base artifact store regardless of which mode 4 flags are on. This is **correct, not a gap**: source text isn't a PLAN-04 entity (no `am_*` mapper for it, no reason to build one), it's a file, and mode 4's own toggle only ever applies to the 7 real facets. Confirmed working end to end earlier this session (§ mode-4 wrap-up: `/source/ANALYZER.ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE.sql` returns real content, 200, under mode 4).

**JAR side — a genuinely different architecture, confirmed by reading `DecompilerService`/`DecompileController` directly**: JAR decompilation is **on-demand, not persisted**. `DecompilerService.decompile()` materializes the whole stored `.jar` to a local temp file per request and runs the decompiler live — its own comment states "Caches nothing." No individual `.java` source document is ever written back to the artifact store. This means the JAR side doesn't have an equivalent of PL/SQL's "one file per source object, stored once" model at all today — every source view is a fresh decompile.

**Recommendation, not yet implemented — this section is a proposal for the user to approve**:
1. **PL/SQL**: no change needed. The existing per-key design already satisfies the stated goal in all 4 modes, verified against real data.
2. **JAR**: if per-class decompiled source needs to be persisted (for speed, or to make it available the same way as PL/SQL's sources), add a genuinely new capability — one `ArtifactKey` per decompiled class (e.g. `jar/<id>/decompiled/<className>.java`), written once on first request and served from the store thereafter, following the exact same per-key pattern PL/SQL sources already use — not a new architecture, just extending the existing `DecompilerService`/`DecompileController` to write-through after decompiling instead of discarding the result. GridFS engages automatically and per-file if any single decompiled class happens to exceed 1 MiB (rare, but some generated/obfuscated classes could); this needs no special-casing given the existing store's own threshold logic.
3. This JAR caching change is real, separate, new work — not attempted in this section, since the user's ask here was for a plan, not implementation.

**Counts after this section**: no registry row transition — this is a design proposal, not a completed task.

### §182 — real, live mode-4 bug found and fixed by actual UI use: `detailFile` missing broke procedure click-through entirely

**Found by the user actually using the live app** (mode 4 fully enabled), not by any of this session's own facet-comparison tests — reported as "source code not visible when I click on proc name, nothing is coming" and "some information near proc name and the Direct/Subtree/SubFlow/Full scope toggle is coming empty."

**Root cause, confirmed directly, not assumed**: `EntityProceduresReader` (§154/§155) was verified only against `ParserFacetSpecs.PROCEDURES`'s own field usage — the grid's own row shape. It was never checked against the *other* real consumer of the same `/procedures` endpoint's data: `parser/js/app.js`'s `PA.showProcedure`, which builds `PA.nodeIndex` from this exact response and then reads each node's `detailFile` to fetch the full per-node detail (source, rich counts, variables) via `GET /node/{file}.json` — a separate endpoint, always artifact-backed, confirmed still working correctly on its own. Without `detailFile`, `PA.showProcedure`'s `if (detailFile)` branch never ran at all — no source fetch, no `PA.context.procDetail`, no `PA.context.scopedTables` — which explains **both** reported symptoms from one shared cause: the detail header/proc-name-adjacent info and the scope-toggle-dependent screens (`Direct`/`Subtree`/`SubFlow`/`Full`) all read from `PA.context.procDetail`/`scopedTables`, both set only inside that same skipped block.

Confirmed via direct HTTP comparison: `?source=artifact`'s response already had `detailFile: "nodes/ANALYZER$ERP_USP_RUN_CYCLE.json"`; the default (entity) response had no `detailFile` field at all. **This bug does not reproduce with mode 4 off** — artifact-scan mode never lost this field.

**Fix**: added `sourceFile`, `lineStart`, `lineEnd` (free — already on `am_proc_node`) and a computed `detailFile` (`"nodes/" + nodeId + ".json"`, matching the real convention confirmed against this corpus's own artifact-scan output) to `EntityProceduresReader`. Once `detailFile` is present, the existing, unmodified merge logic in `PA.showProcedure` does the rest — no client-side change needed.

**Known, stated limitation, not silently assumed away**: for a package analysis, the artifact path's own `detailFile` can point into a proc subfolder (`IndexFacetReader.getProcedures`'s own package-analysis enrichment); this simple top-level construction does not reproduce that. Not exercised by this repo's own standalone-entrypoint corpus, and not fixed here — a real, separate follow-up if a package analysis is ever run under entity-read mode.

**Calibration**: added `everyRowCarriesTheDetailFileTheClientNeedsToFetchFullDetail` to `EntityProceduresReaderComparisonTest` (3 tests total now). Broke the `detailFile` computation (`if (false && ...)`), confirmed the exact expected failure (`expected: <nodes/...json> but was: <>`), restored, reconfirmed clean.

**Verified live, end to end**: rebuilt, restarted the app with both mode-4 flags on, confirmed `detailFile` now present in the default `/procedures` response. Full JS suite: 307/307. Full Java reactor: confirmed clean (see log).

**A real, useful lesson for the rest of this session's facet-comparison discipline**: verifying a reader only against its own facet's declared field usage is not sufficient when the same underlying artifact-scan endpoint is *also* consumed elsewhere for a different purpose with a different field need. This is worth checking for the other 6 converted facets too — not done in this pass, a real follow-up.

### §183 — call-graph "two root nodes" bug: real root cause found and fixed (`DependencyCrawler` from-side overload arity)

**Reported by the user**: "graph screen have two root nodes why?" — part of the same live-use bug
report as §182. Confirmed directly on the real corpus, not assumed: `/call-graph` showed
`ANALYZER$ERP_PKG_PLANNER$COMPUTE_TOTAL` (no arity suffix) as a second root — a phantom id matching
no real node (the real overloaded node exists only as `COMPUTE_TOTAL__1`/`__2`), unresolvable even
via `node_id_map.json`'s own documented "resolve edge references" mechanism (no key for the bare id
exists in that map at all).

**Root cause, in `DependencyCrawler.addCallEdge`**: the `toNodeId` side of every edge already
appended an overload-arity suffix via a `toOverloadArity` parameter; the `fromNodeId` side never
did. When an overloaded node (e.g. `COMPUTE_TOTAL__2`) is itself the source of an outgoing call, its
own edge-side id was built without the disambiguation that would match a real node — a
**pre-existing bug**, confirmed not a MID-026 regression (MID-026 converted `writeCallGraph`'s own
loop shape but never touched `DependencyCrawler`'s edge-building logic, which is where the asymmetry
actually lives).

**Fix**: added a `fromOverloadArity` parameter to `addCallEdge`, mirroring the existing
`toOverloadArity` handling exactly, fed by the current BFS item's own already-computed
`isOverloaded`/`item.argCount` (the node being processed is always the "from" side of every edge it
emits) — threaded through all 4 `enqueueExternalCalls` call sites.

**Verified live**: rebuilt, restarted (mode 4), re-ran the real Oracle analysis, fetched
`/call-graph`: 218 edges, 0 phantom node ids (every `fromNodeId`/`toNodeId` cross-checked against
the real 52-node `/procedures` set), exactly 1 true root. `COMPUTE_TOTAL__2 -> COMPUTE_TOTAL__1`
now carries the correctly suffixed `fromNodeId`.

**Calibrated**: reverted the fix, rebuilt, re-ran — reproduced the exact reported bug (2 roots, the
same phantom id, 2 phantom edges). Restored, rebuilt clean, reconfirmed 1 root.

**Full `plsql-parser` suite**: 748/748. **Full reactor**: one unrelated failure
(`IngestMainModeAwareSourceTest`, a real-corpus-data-fixture-dependent test whose assumed
pre-existing gap no longer reproduces after this pass's own repeated live re-runs of the same
analysis — not touched by this fix, flagged honestly rather than silently ignored; see log §183).

**Status: DONE.**

### §184 — §182's own follow-up: audited the other 6 mode-4 entity readers against every real frontend consumer, not just their own facet's declared grid fields; found and fixed 2 real gaps

Following §182's own stated lesson directly ("worth checking for the other 6 converted facets too — not done in this pass, a real follow-up"): for each of `EntityTablesReader`, `EntityJoinsReader`, `EntityCursorsReader`, `EntitySequencesReader`, `EntityPredicatesReader`, `EntityDynamicSqlReader`, found every real frontend file that reads a field off that facet's row (not just `ParserFacetSpecs`'s own declared grid usage — the same class of consumer `PA.showProcedure` was for `/procedures`), and cross-checked every field each one actually reads.

**Already fully correct, no change needed:**
- `EntityCursorsReader` — `parser/js/cursors.js` reads exactly `cursorName, cursorType, queryText, accessCount, accessDetails[].{operation,procedureId,procedureName,lineNumber,sourceFile}`, all already present.
- `EntitySequencesReader` — `parser/js/sequences.js` reads exactly `sequenceName, sequenceSchema, accessCount, operations, accessDetails[].{operation,procedureId,procedureName,lineNumber,sourceFile}`, all already present.
- `EntityPredicatesReader` — `plsql/js/predicates.js` (the real consumer; dispatches to the parser backend by `_parserName()`, same pattern `tableOps.js`'s own doc comment describes) reads `tableName, schemaName, tableType, predicateCount, predicates[].columnName` (`uniqueColumns` is computed client-side from `predicates`, not read off the row), all already present.
- `EntityDynamicSqlReader` — `parser/js/dynamicSql.js` reads `procedureId, procedureName, lineNumber, sourceFile, sqlExpression, type, usingVariables`; `usingVariables` looked missing on a first field-name grep (only checked `.put(`/`.set(` calls) but is in fact already emitted via `.putArray("usingVariables")` — confirmed correct, not a gap.

**Real gap #1 — `EntityTablesReader` missing `triggers` (found via `parser/js/tableOps.js`, not `ParserFacetSpecs.TABLES`, which never reads it):** `tableOps.js`'s own "Triggers" grid column (`(t.triggers || []).length`) and detail-panel trigger section both read `t.triggers` directly off the table row; `EntityTablesReader` never emitted it at all — every table would silently show a 0 trigger count and an empty trigger section under entity-read mode. Root cause: there is no `am_table` catalogue collection to hang triggers off (per this class's own doc comment on the join shape) — the real per-trigger data lives in `am_db_object__triggers`, keyed by `parentRef`, matching `am_node_table_access`'s own `objectRef` field exactly (confirmed against the real corpus: `ORACLE~ANALYZER~ERP_BOM_HEADER`-shaped key on both sides). Fixed by capturing `objectRef` on the existing `AccessRow` (free — already read) and joining it to `am_db_object__triggers`, reproducing the source-parsed trigger shape (`nodeId, name, schema, event, timing`). **Known, stated limitation:** DB-discovered trigger enrichment (`status`, `tableOps`, `definition`) is written straight onto the artifact by the crawler with no ingest mapper of its own — not exercised by this corpus (0 DB-discovered trigger rows here, confirmed directly), not fixed here.

**Real gap #2 — `EntityJoinsReader`'s `accessDetails[]` missing per-occurrence `joinType` and `sourceFile` (found via `parser/js/joins.js`'s `_renderDetail`/`toggleSql`, not `ParserFacetSpecs.JOINS`):** each join occurrence badge reads `d.joinType` (colour/label — `"? JOIN"` and the muted "unknown" colour otherwise) and `d.sourceFile` (the "Show SQL" fallback source, when the node-detail fetch itself doesn't carry one); the reader only emitted the pair-level `joinTypes[]` (already correct and unrelated) and never a per-detail `joinType`/`sourceFile`. Fixed: `JoinRow` already carried `joinType()`; added it per detail. `sourceFile` added by fetching it off `am_proc_node` alongside the display name already being batched there (free, same query).
